speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext:
I should like to
raise a question or two on this resolution. When other departments of government have been before the committee it has been stated that we are receiving this year $255 million on our grain crops alone less than we would

Income War Tax

receive in, the open markets of the world if there were no controls. I know this is not directly relevant to the resolution under discussion, but it is a lead to what I have to say. We have wheat participating certificates which pay us in 1946 for our 1943 production. That is three years later, and we are not allowed any interest even though the wheat producer may have to borrow money on which to operate. On the other hand, when he pays his income tax he is always charged interest on overdue payments. I cite that as an example. Added to this, we are taking 40 to 50 per cent less for our live stock, and we have the greatest production and the greatest sale in the history of this nation. We are selling this live stock at from 40 to 50 per cent less than the world market price. The point I am coming to is the matter of a breeding herd being allowed as capital. I know this question has been raised in other sessions. Suppose a man is going out on a mixed farm or a grain farm; he buys land and equipment, and it is allowed as capital. But take a man who has a ranch where there is no other income than that which is derived from the live stock. He purchases a herd of breeding cows. If he is forced to sell that herd, even through no fault of his own, in one year, the entire herd must be shown as income. I submit that is a most unfair ruling. I know the breeders of this country have interviewed the government on past occasions. They have asked that the breeding stock be all shown as capital, which was disallowed. Finally, they asked that they be allowed at least 75 per cent of their breeding cattle as capital. .
I came back from the west not very many days ago. I met a rancher who had sold out in southern Alberta. He received some sixty odd thousand dollars for his herd. Those were the only assets that man had. He, his wife and family, had spent all their life accumulating this herd. He thought he was going to settle down in town and enjoy his old age. I do not know that I need to go into any further details to explain to the committee the headache which that man had when he interviewed the income tax officials. I think that is an impossible situation. Because of these controls the producers of this country have been forced to take a real licking during the war years, and certainly I believe they are entitled to more consideration in the matter of income tax, especially in connection with the older people, many of whom wish to retire. After having made a great effort during the war years; after having accumulated a fair herd of good stock, now when they come 
to sell they are not allowed to keep enough of the proceeds to provide for their old age.
In raising that point I should like to mention also the other question of the farmer and his wife as compared with the man and his wife who work in the city. The farmer and his wife are allowed an exemption of only $1,200, or whatever it is, while the -man and his wife working in the city are allowed an exemption of something like $1,800. That has been a most vexing problem throughout the rural parts of Canada, and if the minister has not brought about some adjustment already I hope he will be able to do so soon.
These are the two particular points I should like to bring to his attention now, and I should be glad to have him' explain them as to date.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The farmer who is paying income tax on a cash basis as distinguished from an inventory basis is taxed on the proceeds of the sale of his stock, which is regarded as gross income, just as any expenditures he makes for stock are regarded as expenses. If the man about whom the hon. gentleman talks had been buying cattle during the last few years every purchase he made would have been regarded as an expense which he could deduct from his income for tax purposes! Then when he comes to sell his cattle what he gets is regarded as income for tax purposes. There is a way of setting up the books on a different basis, an inventory basis, as I understand it; and I believe the Department of National Revenue have gone just as far as they could in allowing retroactive adjustments over five years, or something like that. I thought the situation had been reasonably met by administrative rulings, but without departing from all fundamental principles I do not think you could regard as capital the cattle as they are bought and sold.

What happens where
herds have been developed through natural increase, where there has been no purchase? "When they are sold, are the proceeds treated as taxable income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes, just as the expenses of feeding them and securing that natural increase are regarded as deductible expenses. The difference is what the farmer makes out of raising cattle; that is his profit.

The minister suggested that there might be some means of spreading the profit, as in the case just mentioned by the hon. member for Souris, over a number of years. If a herd has been developed over a period of, let us say twenty years, and it

Income War Tax
is necessary to allocate the proceeds to each of the past twenty years, surely the interest on the amounts that have been owing since the beginning of the period would run to such a figure that in the result there would be very little relief for the taxpayer.

Could the minister explain this in some detail? As he will realize, now that the war is over, many people who' worked hard to produce for the war effort are getting on in years and wish to sell out and retire. With the experience some of their neighbours have had,'they are rather fearful about it. To be asked to submit the proceeds of their sales to the department for a ruling is hardly satisfactory. There must be some basis on which this is worked out, and I should like the minister to explain that in some detail. Take an arbitrary figure of $10,000 or $20,000 and spread it over the maximum number of years to show how it would work out. That would give useful information to many people. That figure may be too high, but take some figure and give us an example. Could the minister do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not immediately, but I can do so later on. That comes under the Department of National Revenue, and I will get a statement from them.

Following up this question,
I should like to point out to the minister that it is difficult to accept his general statement that breeding cattle cannot be regarded as capital, because if you analyse the position I think it is fair to say that a farmer needs a certain proportion of his herd to carry on his business, just as much as any other business man needs capital assets before he can earn an income. In the case of those who confine their agriculture almost entirely to the breeding and sale of beef cattle it is not only their land and buildings that form part of their equipment but also a certain percentage of their herds, because if they did not have that herd in the first place they would not have any annual increase which they could sell and from which they derive their income. Therefore, if you analyse it and compare it with any other business you will see that a portion of the herd must be kept from year to year in order to have any crop at all to sell, and surely it is fair to say that this portion of the herd should be regarded as working capital. One might say it is all the female animals in the herd, though perhaps that is setting it too high. The figure suggested by the hon. member for Souris is seventy-five per cent. In any event we are not concerned here with such details, nor 47696-173J
should we demand that these matters be worked out at this moment. I know, however, that the Department of Agriculture has submitted a brief or a recommendation on this subject to the Department of National Revenue. Apparently as yet the details have not been worked out between the two departments, but in view of that recommendation I earnestly hojie the minister will give this matter his serious consideration and see if some fair basis cannot be worked out by the time next year's budget is brought down.
The minister mentioned that some relief is given at the moment by averaging up profits and losses over the years. I was in communication with the Department of National Revenue yesterday, and this cau be done in two ways. One is by going on what is called the cash basis. A man pays perhaps $10,000 for the purchase of a herd of cattle and he is allowed to deduct that amount from his income. That is the basis of his herd. The proceeds from anything he sells from then on are regarded as income, on which he pays a tax, even though he might sell the whole herd again. The other way is to go on the inventory basis: to establish the value of the herd as-at a specific time, and then from year to year declare either an increase or a decrease in that value and pay the tax on the increase whether or not you sell. That goes part way toward meeting what we suggest, because to some extent it recognizes that a certain proportion of the herd is working capital, and you pay income tax on the increase over that from year to year. But in order to do that a farmer has to go back to 1935 and very few farmers in the west, particularly those who went through the depression years, have their records back that far. They have to establish their herd back to the basis of 1935, and that is almost impossible. But it is a beginning; and in recognizing that principle I suggest to the minister he is recognizing actually the principle that a certain proportion of the farmer's herd of cattle, namely his breeding stock, is capital and not income.
I should like to say a word about the seriousness of this matter. On Tuesdey in this chamber one hon. member made some remarks, which I do not believe were intended in any sense to be derogatory, about farmers who are always complaining. This, perhaps, is not so important at the present time, because to-day farmers are' relatively prosperous. I am in no sense denying that. They are now in the income tax group, and they are paying taxes. Everyone is pleased aboqt that. But may I remind hon. members who would sometimes believe that farmers complain too much, that those farmers do not get workmen's compen-
Income War Tax

sation. A farmer will go through bad times and good times; but in the bad times he will not go on strike.
Order.

He will continue to produce, and even though times may be bad' he will not get compensation or unemployment relief. I would ask hon. members to bear that in mind when to-day, in good times, vre ask for some relief on their behalf from income tax.
The ACTING CHAIRMAN (Mr. Golding); Order. I believe I shall have to read the resolution again. It states:
(a) That in respect of persons other than corporations the tax for 1945 be reduced by 4 per cent of the aggregate of the normal tax, the graduated tax and the investments surtax.

My intention was to emphasize that what I have said is serious, and it is a situation which is felt keenly by a large section of our population. I do not think I need emphasize it further.
Might I close by saying that this condition affects a large number of the primary producers of this country. Now that they are being taxed, they do not ask for more than they feel is due them, but they do ask to be put on a fair tax basis which will allow them, when times are good, to expect no more or to be under no greater obligation than when times are bad. In this way they will be able to even up the situation between good times and bad.

May I direct the attention of the committee to the class of farmers who, I believe, are most adversely affected by this resolution. I do not believe the commercial breeders or the large ranchers are most adversely affected. My impression is that there is a regulation permitting them to keep their books on a different basis, and to take care of themselves in that way. But there is a group of farmers who are not able to take advantage of those regulations. I refer to those average farmers who build their herds, not through purchasing but through breeding on their own farms over a number of years. Perhaps in those years they have never had great increases in their herds which - would place them in the income tax group. Over a period of twenty years they may have accumulated considerable Stock. One of those farmers may want to retire, and to sell his stock. There are dozens of farmers in Canada in that position to-day. Many of them carried on during the war longer than they should have. Now they want to retire, and they find that if they dispose of their stock, a con-

siderable portion of the return will be taken by the income tax people, even though the accumulation of that stock has been spread over a number of years, and in those years it has not been taxable. I think this is unfair, especially in those cases where a man would not normally have paid a tax during the years in which he was accumulating his stock.
However, now when he sells he finds that he has to pay perhaps twenty-five per cent, thirty per cent or forty per cent of the sate value. I suggest that the minister should introduce a regulation whereby perhaps seventy-five per cent of those sales would not be taxable. The present situation is certainly not fair, and is causing a great deal of discontent and dissatisfaction, particularly among the average farmers who have accumulated their herds throughout the years. I hope the minister, through his department, will give some thought to this group of people.

Much of what I had intended to say has already been said by the hon. member for Melfort, and the hon. member who preceded him. I wish only to endorse what they have said.
However, there is another class of primary producers concerning whom I should like to say a few words. I refer to the fishermen who produce fish, from our fresh water lakes in Manitoba, and the other provinces. They have heavy capital expenditures. I have known some of them to provide 200 or 300 fishing nets and, after placing them in the water, to have them frozen in the ice. Then, with warm weather coming along, probably about this time of the year, the ice will break up and their nets will be swept away. I do not know whether there is anything in this resolution which would give them relief in respect of their loss of capital equipment-because nets are undoubtedly in that class. In the past they have suffered heavy losses by having to provide new nets. When their catches are good, however, they still have to pay income tax.
I wish also to refer to the tax relief of sixteen per cent of the aggregate of the normal tax, the graduated tax and the investment surtax. In this connection I believe there are two things which are not right. It is our belief that the income tax exemption level should have been raised. This would have been a more effective way of giving relief to those in the lower income brackets who need it most. Under the present arrangement they will obtain less benefit.
Second, we believe that the income tax relief should be graduated so as to give those in the lower brackets greater relief from the

Income War Tax
tax than is given those in the higher brackets. I shall not say more at this time. I do not expect that what I have said will have any great effect, but it was my wish to register this protest.
Would the minister indicate how he feels in this matter?

Mr. MoMASTER: I come from a city, but I am wondering what the difference is, in principle, between a farmer who sells out his whole stock and assets, and a man in the city who sells his hardware business, or any other business. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member is talking about selling a building, that would be different from selling stock in trade.
I mean stock in trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Almost every business man is on an inventory basis. At the - end of the year if the value has gone up, that is a profit and he is taxed. If it goes up some more the next year, there is more profit. If it goes down, there is a loss. But he has paid as he
has gone along and when he sells out the whole thing he has not much profit in that year upon which to pay income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman talking about a merchant or a farmer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Most farmers are in the business of buying and selling cattle.

No.
Mr. ILSLEYt They are certainly in the business of selling them.
Breeding and selling, not buying and selling.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not make any difference in principle. If he is breeding cattle, he has the expense of raising them. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I stated in the budget speech that I intended to introduce some system of averaging. It is going to be a hard job because you will have to .draw a distinction between classes in .the community. You cannot average everybody. If we are to avoid charges of discrimination we shall have to go very slowly in this. It may be that we can 'take the primary producers, the farmers and the fishermen, put them on one side of the fence and then put everybody else on the other side. .But then we are going to have continual claims from those who consider they are on the wrong side of the fence. That is something we shall have to< face.
They have a system in Australia-I do not know just how it works-whereby they give primary producers a little different treatment. There is a better case for primary producers than there is for anybody else because of the dangers of loss on account of weather and market conditions. In the past, market conditions have not been at all steady, or at least not as steady as they have been in most other businesses. But it is only a matter of degree. There are a lot of businessmen who have had their years of losses and their years of low profits and perhaps years of high profits without any averaging. During the war with the high taxes we have gone part way in allowing losses to be written off against profits of the previous year or against profits of the three following years, and that applies to farmers as well as to everybody else. But that system is objected to on the ground that there may never be a year of loss; there may be years of just small profits, as in the case of these cattle producers. These men will go on without selling very much. They will continue to buy but will not be in the income tax category. Then suddenly the time will come when they want to sell a lot and then they must pay income tax that year. They are put into the higher brackets by that transaction. I understand that the Australian system is to keep them in an average bracket or something like that. I am determined that we are going to do something like that if we can work it out.

I am very grateful to hear the minister make the statement he has to-day and the one he made on the budget. As he has suggested, consideration will have to be given to this whole problem, not only the problem of taxation but the complete picture. We must have-a proper policy for agriculture as a whole, because it cannot go on in the future on the basis it has been forced to operate on in the past,

If you look back over the depression years you will see the losses that have been suffered by our farmers when they had to work year in and year out and hardly made their expenses. We are supposed to have been making profits since the war broke out, but I think it will be found that most of those supposed profits have been used to pay debts that were contracted during or before the depression years. I should like to see a period of five years taken as a basis for fixing profits in the case of farmers.
I wish to suggest raising the exemption for both single and married people. I would urge also a reduction in the income tax. I think the minister realizes that in the period after the war" the people must have purchasing power if our industries are to be kept busy and be able to take care of our unemployment problem.

Dealing with the unfairness of the present method of taxing the sale of cattle, I should like to cite one instance. I have in mind a man who lives near my home. For the past twenty or twenty-five years he has been a successful farmer. He bought farms for four or five of his children and he owns several himself. If he sold any of those farms the proceeds would not be taxable. If, instead of buying land, he had put his profits into the purchase of stock and thdta. sold those cattle, the proceeds would be taxable. There are many farmers in my district who are under a great handicap. They are getting on in years and during their lifetime they have built up a considerable herd. If they sell their herds most of the profits would go to the income tax department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If he puts his money into cattle instead of into farms he would have reduced his income tax that year to a marked extent because it would have been treated as an expense.
I think I ought to say in .reference to working out some system of averaging for farmers and fishermen that it will be a complicated arrangement, and members of the house who object to complexity and espouse simplicity will be disappointed. It will not be possible to get in and out either; there will be a great temptation to want to average sometimes and not at others. There will have to be an element of rigidity about it, as well as an element of complexity. All this is entirely unavoidable.

speechtext: This is a resolution affecting tax liability, not the method of collecting the tax, but I have no objection to my hon. friend discussing what he has in mind.

speechtext: I would be willing to give consideration to a system of that kind. I was under the impression, although I am told by the officials that I am wrong, that they have enacted something of that kind in the United States. I do not know whether that is so or not. A system of that kind would be convenient but it would not be just.

I think the minister has in mind the suggestion made by a senate committee in the United States that that system be adopted. But I do not think it has as yet been put into force.
Another matter I should like to discuss is one that I have mentioned more than once before, and that is in regard to the portion of the 1942 tax which has not been paid. I will read the item:
The deferred tax portion (if any) item 5, in respect of investment income in excess of $3,000, becomes due on, and is thereby deferred until the date of the taxpayer's death,.with interest from that date at 8 per cent per annum until paid, unless the taxpayer elected to pay and paid on or before 30th April, 1944, at a 2 per cent per annum life expectancy discount.
I would suggest in regard to these taxes that have not been paid on 1942 income that they be allowed to be paid at any date at the same rate that prevailed before, two per cent per annum life expectancy discount, but that when the taxpayer dies his estate should be allowed at least six months. In the United States I believe they allow fifteen months. Six months at least should be allowed, and then after that date charge interest, although I think eight per cent is too high.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It runs from the exact date of death, does it?

Yes, interest at eight per' cent per annum has to be paid from the date of death. The minister knows that the estate cannot pay it on that day and many estates cannot pay it for many, many months because there are succession duties and this, that, and
the other thing to look after. Personally I owe a little myself. I do not know what my estate would do. It might have a hard time getting any money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the suggestion is well worthy of consideration. I did not realize that the penalty rate started so promptly.

I brought this matter up when we were discussing the income tax last year and the Minister of National Revenue, now the Minister for Air, I believe said that I was wrong. I hunted up my tax bills and I know I am right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree with the first part of my hon>. friend's suggestion that the taxpayers have an option to pay at any time before their death because they pay on a discount basis, the discount being on their life expectancy. The only thing to do in cases of that kind is to fix a date beyond which they can take their option. We may have fixed the date too early, but I do not think so. It was stated in the house that they have a year and a half to two years to exercise this option, and a lot of them did. I do not think I would extend that date. They can pay any time if they want to.
Yes, they can pay any time, but not with advantage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not on a discount basis, no.

The reason I bring this matter to the minister's attention is that, as he knows, we have had good times and there is the chance that many of those who owe money to the government might in another five or ten years not have a nickel when they die, so that when they die the government would not get a cent. The minister knows that. There is a chance that some of these taxpayers will be absolutely flat broke when they die and the government will be out just that much. That is why I suggest that this be extended for at least a further period, I have made a few suggestions and I'hope the minister will look into them. I hope he will look into deducting 100 per cent of the income tax at the source from wages and then forget about the return which the wage-earner is supposed to make in the following year.

I just want one question in my own mind clarified because it is a question that we are often asked in connection with the tax on farming. I understand from what the minister said that if the farmer proceeds on the inventory basis from year to year he pays his income tax on his increase in inventory as though it were income. But if he has a farm sale, will the farm sale be
Income Tf'ar Tax

subject to tax? Will he be in the same classification then as the hardware merchant if he is paying on the inventory basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he has paid on the increment each year in the value of his herd he does not have to pay on the total value of the herd when it is sold.

When we were talking about the treatment of married couples for taxation purposes, I have in mind the case of the farmer and his wife who work on the farm. There was the distinction that the farmer and his wife were allowed an exemption of only $1,200, whereas the couple working in the city were granted an exemption of $1,800. I was wondering whether the minister has found any way of dealing with that situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I know exactly what I intend to do about it. I do not know whether it is policy to state it.
Can we be hopeful?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The concession we made in
1942 was essentially a concession to war workers, to get married women to work in war factories. When a single taxpayer's exemption was put down to $660 the penalty upon a married couple in a city, each of whom worked in a factoly, was very great when the married woman earned more than $660, because she then put her husband from the married status into the single status; in many cases he had to pay several hundred dollars more a year in taxes, and they started to leave the factories in very substantial numbers. We just had to change it, as a war necessity.
So that we can guess what the minister is going to do now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is wrong in principlethere is no doubt about that-and it will have to be changed. When a man is in receipt of a higher exemption because his wife is dependent upon him although in fact his wife is not dependent upon him, he should, of course, lose that exemption. We could not do that in time of war so that we passed the law we did. We have gone over this argument here time after time. But that is the way in which I expect to be meeting the situation, before too long; I do not know whether it will be in 1946 or not, but it was all gone into at the time we prepared the budget. I do, not agree with the reasoning behind the hon. member's argument. I believe that if we were to grant what is asked for, that is if we were to allow farmers to pay their wives $660 a year because they work on the farm) it would not be a month before we 	* ;	:
would be driven into allowing everybody to do the same thing, and we would just be increasing the married man's exemption to that extent all along the line. I do not think we can do that.

Not only that, but a lot of
wives would demand it. The minister had better leave it alone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think that can
possibly be done, and I think the other will have to be done.

I have been trying to find a place to ask about single and married status for income tax purposes depending on circumstances of residence. I might give as an example the case of an unmarried lady, a schoolteacher. She and her sister live in her own home. She supports the invalid sister and accordingly, I believe, receives marriage status. Circumstances in connection with her qualification may cause her to lose her position in that city and compel her to go to another town and board there. She still owns her home in the city and maintains her invalid sister in that home. According to a ruling of the income tax department she is therefore placed in the status of a single person. This seems to be a hardship. I have taken up the case with income tax officials, and they so admit, but apparently they have no discretion in the matter. They promised that the case would be brought to the attention of the department. I think it is a matter of principle and justice: it may be difficult from an administrative point of view; nevertheless in justice she should be granted the married status.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That cannot be done under
the law as it stands now, and i must say I do not see any way in which we could change the law so that it could be done, because there is a big difference between the obligations assumed by a person who has a self-contained domestic establishment and by one who has not. All I can do is give consideration to the hon. gentleman's representations. I do not anticipate that any change in the law can be made this session.

The question I wish to ask is perhaps more directly concerned with the Ministry of National Revenue than the Ministry of Finance. I understand that there is some regulation whereby part of the farmer's income, say the portion received from the poultry flock where the wife is taking care of the poultry, may not be included in his tax return as income. I am wondering just where the department draw the line with

Income War Tax
respect to that. On one1 farm is a poultry flock of a hundred head, where the income is not very large; on another farm a thousand hens may be kept and the income may be quite large. I should like the Minister of National Revenue to indicate where they draw the line with respect to the amount which may be taken from the farmer's income with respect to special lines such as poultrykeeping or, say, bee-keeping, or maybe where they milk only two or three cows, on a grain farm, and where the cream cheque goes to the woman and is not included in the income of the farmer himself.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: It has been the custom of the department to allow the income from a small partial occupation on a farm such as the hon. member has indicated to go as income to the wife. But it will all depend on what that proportion is to the whole operations of the farm. For instance, if they start out in that way and finally develop into an entirely poultry-raising farm, that becomes the chief occupation of the husband.
Has the department established certain percentages? I want to get at where the line is drawn.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: No, it is not laid down as a certain percentage. It depends in the individual case entirely upon the weight- we may call it-or proportion which that bears to the total income of that particular farm.
I think there should be some definite percentage or weight to go by; otherwise it will be entirely subject to the discretion of some, departmental official who may be fair in all cases, or may not.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: What does the hon. member suggest?

I think the percentage
should be fixed.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: What does the hon. member suggest As a percentage?

I am not going to make a suggestion. The Minister of National Revenue knows the circumstances much better than I do and knows the intention of the government with respect to this provision. I do not know whether it is the intention of the government to place the farmer's wife in the same position, say, as the woman who is working .in industry whom the Minister of Finance has just described. I think there was some suggestion that that is what the department were doing when they made this regulation, and I want to get the thing clarified so that people will know just what they can 47696-174
and cannot do under this provision, because I know there is a tremendous variation in what has been done under it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: No better system has been found of doing it than to weigh each individual case and do what we consider to be fair. As I have said, if it becomes the chief line on that particular farm then it goes in as income for the owner who is in most cases the man.

What consideration is being given to men who came to Canada in the late thirties, settled here and took out their naturalization certificate, and who have families in the old land? I have had several of those cases brought to my attention, and in each case the individual was taxed as a single man. Cpuld not some consideration be given to these people, particularly at the present time when they have to send money and assistance to members of their families in Europe?

The point raised by the hon. member has caused a good deal of anxiety among certain residents of Canada who are in the exact position which he has mentioned. They have been supporting their families in Europe at such times as they could send remittances there, and when they could not do so they made other provision for those families. They do feel keenly that no allowance has been given them in the matter of income taxes. I know one instance very well, and I feel that the man is labouring under a disadvantage which probably cannot be helped under the existing legislation. However, it is still unfair and places him in an embarrassing position.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: That is not a great problem to handle, because any married man who for income tax purposes claims married status and can prove to the satisfaction of the department that he is a married man is taxed at the rate for a married man. If those people of foreign birth, who have, as they claim, a wife in some other country, will produce a certificate t!o that effect, supported by an affidavit, it is usually accepted; or if they will go to the consul of the country from which they came and obtain a certificate from him to the effect that So-and-so is a married man, that is accepted and1 he is taxed accordingly; or he is given the allowance which he should be given as a married person.

In that connection I have many of those cases and in not one instance was any exemption allowed. The income tax inspector would usually refuse and say to him: "Well, you have no proof that you have been

Income War Tax

helping your family, and during the past five years while the war was on you could not be helping your family." That is final. He has no place to go. He cannot appeal from the income tax inspector's decision in that instance. Would it not be advisable for the minister to send out a circular or inform the various divisions or income tax branches that they should allow such exemption, provided, of course, that these men can prove tiiat they are married, have families and are helping them from time to time. I think that would simplify matters greatly, and, of course, it deserves serious consideration.

Has any thought been given to extending deductions or exemptions to second generations? A great many young people went away to war and married. They returned. They are handicapped in earning a livelihood because they are unprepared at the present time for their life's work. They are going to school; they are undergoing training and they have lusty broods of children. The parent of the soldier is supporting those grandchildren who are dependent upon him to the same extent as his own children were twenty or twenty-five years ago. It seems to me that there is a big category of dependents who are overlooked by the statute in its present form.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: That is already provided for in the act and in the regulations. If it is indicated and proven that a grandchild is dependent upon a man's parent for its support, the grandparent gets exemption in that regard in his income tax return.

The proof of matters of this kind must, of course, be submitted to the department. But I think it is generally [DOT] accepted that so long as the parent is alive the grandchild is not a charge upon the grandparent, although most frequently and inevitably for some years the grandchild is and will, in fact be such a charge.
The question of double taxation has been brought to my attention by-
Would the hon. gentleman let me get an answer to my question, please?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
I think this section covers the question of the hon. member. It reads as follows:
A taxpayer may deduct from the normal tax otherwise payable by him in any year under this section 28 for each person who was during that year wholly dependent upon that taxpayer and was ... his grandchild.
Then there are a lot of others included. Jt goes on:

. . . except such dependent person by reason of whom such person is taxable under rule 1 of this section who being a taxpayer employs a fulltime housekeeper or servant in a self-contained domestic establishment where he supports a child by reason of whom he is taxable under rule 1 of the section, he may not notwithstanding the exception contained in this rule make the deduction permitted under this rule for all the dependents described by him.

I do not think that covers it. It says, "wholly dependent", and the soldier who has dependents and is going to college at present gets a certain allowance from the government for each child. The child could not be considered as wholly dependent. The phrase "wholly dependent" would shut him out of the income tax deduction.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The child is probably not dependent upon the grandparent at all, if the child's own father has sufficient income to keep him.	-

The question of double taxation of income has been brought to my attention on a few occasions. By that I mean that a person working in the United States pays income tax on the earnings he made there for part of the year. He then comes back to Canada and earns some more money. He pays tax here; but in addition to paying tax on his earnings in Canada he is also compelled to pay tax on the amount earned in the United States. Is that correct? Why should that Canadian who has already paid tax on his United States earnings be compelled to pay income tax on the whole amount in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He pays a tax on the entire income because he is resident in Canada for part of the year, but he gets credit for that part of the tax which is payable in the United States.

I did not understand it in that way. Two parties who brought this matter to my attention claimed they had to pay the full tax without getting any credit. If that is the case I think the department should see to it that the credit is given.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

There is a point in connection with the forms to be used for the payment of income tax which I wanted to take up with the minister. Since income tax has become heavier in recent years, more and more individuals and business people have had recourse to the assistance of accountants. One such accountant in Vernon, British Columbia, puts a point to me which he thinks has not been mentioned so far, in these words:

Income War Tax
Reference to company form T-2 discloses that a company receives a clear six months to file their form from the close of their business year, and as far as I am aware are always able to use the last form printed.
Now, how about the unincorporated individual. He neither knows what the form T-l general is going to be like nor when it will be printed
In my humble opinion, proprietors and partnerships should be treated equally and should have six months to file their form T-l general from the time they are available to the public and in no case less than six months from1 January 1 unless they are available by December 1. An increasing number of taxpayers are requesting services from accountants which they are unable to give and the disparity in time is very unfair.
This particular accountant has previously raised matters in connection with the forms that have to be used, and I remember that last year there was a delay in the printing of the forms. His grievance is that in many instances the accountant is unable to give service to his client because he has not time to do all the work necessary after the printed form becomes available.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: At present the regulations provide that all individuals are given a period of four months from the end of the calendar year. The return must be made by the end of April. With companies the period given is six months. I submit that by far the greater number of individuals do not need and do not use expert people like accountants to make out their returns, and that four months is ample time in which to do so. I do not think giving another couple of months, to the end of June, would either have the forms filled in any better or see any greater number of returns made within the time limit. There are always people who are dilatory in making returns; if you gave them eight or nine months the returns would not come in until the tenth month. That is about the experience of the department in reference to income tax returns. When you establish a deadline of April 30, the people who want to have their returns in by that time will do so. So that I do not believe an extension would be of any great advantage to the individual, and I am sure it would slow up the work of the department in making the assessments.

May I draw the minister's attention to the fact that this complaint partly arises from the fact that the form T-tl general has by no means always been available as early as the end of the fiscal year. If my memory serves me aright, in 1944 the T-l general form was not available in this part of Canada until a very short time before the date it had to be presented.
47696-174;

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I will admit some of that is true, but there are many difficulties in getting out the forms. For instance, the forms for 1945 cannot be put in shape until these resolutions and the bill based upon them actually become law. Then we have the matter of printing difficulties. During the war years particularly, not only the printing bureau but other printing establishments throughout the country whose services we use have been so busy and so short of help that it has been an absolutely physical impossibility to get out the forms as quickly as we would have wished. However, the representations the hon. gentleman has made will be taken into account and we will see if we cannot have the forms out in plenty of time for individuals and companies to make their returns within the time limit.
The minister will agree, I think, that no leeway is given the unfortunate taxpayer who, for the reasons the minister has mentioned, was not able to get hold of a form in time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I will just state this, that the records show that although there are four months in which to make the returns, the great bulk of them are made in the month of April and most of them in the last week, so that lack of forms has not held them up.

I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that the provision which he was kind enough to read, and with which I am not unfamiliar, does not cover the situation I was drawing to his attention. A young man in this position receives a certain amount monthly, which is increased slightly if he is married and to which is added $10 or $12 a month for each child; but that is available to him only during the period of the year he is attending a college or university. It is enough to disqualify the grandparent entirely for any relief under the income tax act, and makes it impossible for the child and grandchild to survive unless they are helped by the grandparents during that portion of the year which is not devoted to study. Of course on the other hand everyone realizes that the assistance given by the government is totally inadequate for the maintenance of those people even during the period they are attending college or university.

There is another group of people I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, although I do not know whether or not he can help them. I refer to settlers who moved from the dried-out. areas into the semi-bush country and who just had
Income War Tax

their first crops about the time they began to get good prices. When they first moved in they put up temporary shacks: I know that last year quite a few wanted to build themselves decent houses, but because they had quite good crops which were worth a good deal of money the income tax was very heavy, and ' they were precluded from building their homes. I was wondering if there was any way of giving these people a little help.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be quite inconsistent with all income tax principles to permit capital expenditure for houses to be regarded as deduction from income for taxation purposes. What I am about to say may not be entirely relevant, but if they w-ere settlers who had suffered losses in the place from which they moved, such losses may now be set off against profits in other years. That is, the loss in-any particular year may be carried back against the profits of the previous year, or against the profits of the three following years. This system has been in force for only a year or two; nevertheless, in cases where there are actual losses there is some mitigation of the rigours of the income tax in years of high profits and high gains. I cannot see any hope of making any change in the law which will allow persons to build houses for themselves out of their profits, and of that being allowed as a deduction for income tax purposes.
This particular group will have to start all over again. They lost practically everything they had.

Has the minister given consideration to the greater decentralization of income tax administration? In British Columbia the administration is centred in Vancouver, and the great majority of the people have no contact with it. I have heard it suggested on many occasions that if the administration were decentralized it would do a great deal to speed up the service of the department, and1 in this way the department would be able to give more satisfactory service and advice to the majority of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
The matter of district reorganization has been under review for the past year. A year ago a committee was set up to study the whole problem with respect to the matter. Ten days or two weeks ago I tabled in the house-and a copy was tabled in the other place-the report of that commission. Although this report has not yet been accepted by the government, there is an outline of a plan for greater district organization from one end of the country to the other. This is done with a view to giving better

service to the public. Then, it will give assistance to some of the offices in the larger centres by the setting up of subdivisions to assist offices which are already overworked.
I am not prepared to make a statement as to the exact location of these new offices until such time as this report has the endorsa-tion of the government. I can only say that the matter is well in band', and that it is the purpose and the aim of the taxation division of , the Department of National Revenue to give the public better service, both by opening up new districts, and by adding to the staff as many competent people as we can get and are needed.

Every year I have referred to these district offices. I hope that an office will be put in Peterborough. Last year one man was sent up there, and was placed in the back of the customs house. Very few people knew he was there.
In many instances the final receipts for income tax payments are not sent out for two or three years. Taxes may be due, but the taxpayer may believe he has made a full payment. Then the govfernment will come along and tell him that he should have paid a tax on this or on that. In my view this condition is not fair to the taxpayer, particularly when he must wait two or three years for his bill, and have included on that bill interest for that length of time. We have noticed that this has happened in the Belleville district, -which serves Peterborough. I must say, however, that that district is served much better since the addition of more staff. I do not think the taxpayer should be charged interest until he gets his bill. It would be proper to make the charge from the time he receives it until the bill is paid. What does the minister think about this?

What is the present position of those persons who have maintained in their homes British refugee children during -the war, and who are still maintaining the-m? Has the department given any consideration to extending income tax deductions to those people? They have been put to a great deal of expense and are worthy of great credit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member is familiar with the history of the situation respecting British children. A distinction was drawn between children from- the United Kingdom who came under a government-sponsored scheme, and those who did not. With regard to the former class some deduction for income tax purposes was allowed the Canadian taxpaper who took these children

Income War Tax
who were moved under an arrangement made between the governments. However, no such deduction was allowed in other cases.
The relevant amendment in 1944 was as follows:
In this act, unless the context otherwise requires, words referring to a child of a taxpayer include
(b) a person who is under 18 years of age and wholly dependent on the taxpayer for support and of 'whom the taxpayer has in law or in fact the custody and control.
That was the first time parliament accepted the principle that a deduction could be allowed in respect of a child who was not a child of the taxpayer, either in fact or by adoption. But since that time a taxpayer may get a deduction in respect of any child who is wholly dependent or, as the section says, any child under eighteen years of age who is wholly dependent on the taxpayer for support, and of whom the taxpayer has in law or in fact the custody and control.
I would suppose that some of the British children who are here are not wholly dependent upon the Canadian taxpayer for support. In that event, if they are only partly dependent, there would not be a deduction. But for those who are wholly dependent the deduction is now allowed.
What is the status for tax purposes of children from the United Kingdom maintained in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know whether there is any special advantage there or not. The provision with regard to government-sponsored transfers of children was never repealed, so far as I recollect. So that the taxpayer who has custody of one of those children has two sections under which he might come. Whether one section is more advantageous than the other, I do not know.
I should like the minister to tell us what he thinks about my suggestion that the interest should not start until the taxpayer receives his account from the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree with it. Here you have one taxpayer who correctly computes his tax liability and pays his money. You have another taxpayer who incorrectly computes his tax liability and keeps part of the money which it is eventually decided should have gone to the crown. The suggestion is that he keep it interest free, and I do not see the equity in that.

I doubt very much whether the minister could probably make out an income tax form and be absolutely correct according'to the decisions of the offices across
the country. Every one of them has a different idea as to the rulings. The matter must come to Ottawa when any one. objects or is not sure; it goes through the office here and eventually gets back to the district office. Perhaps a year or two or three years may elapse. There may be a dispute over an amount that should be payable. I know of one case where there was a difference of $700. The taxpayer thought he was entitled to it, and it was two years before it was decided that he was not entitled to it. I understand that the district office said he was entitled to it but the head office said he was not. When there is any doubt about the matter I do not think the taxpayer should pay interest.
A few moments ago the minister said that it was against the principles of the income tax that deductions should bo allowed for the building of homes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is right.
Mr. lYRIGHT:	When the minister considers the matter of taxation before his next budget I think he should give some consideration to changing that principle. I would suggest that it be done this year, because there is a scarcity of material and it might bring about an increase in the price ceiling, but in another year serious consideration might be given to permitting deductions from income tax for what is spent on the building of a home. We need homes in Canada and we need better homes. It is very difficult for people, especially those in the lower income groups, to acquire a home under our present income tax structure. I am not suggesting that deductions be allowed where a home costing $10,000 or $20,000 or $50,000 is built, but I think serious consideration should be given to allowing some exceptions in the case of the moderate home costing from $5,000 to $7,000. There is a tremendous need for homes of that type; there is a tremendous need for housing on our farms, in our industrial areas and in our towns and villages practically all over ' Canada.

I should like to bring up a matter which perhaps should have been brought up earlier. It has to do with ministers; not ministers of the crown but ministers of the gospel. I believe it has been decided by the income tax authorities that no allowance for an automobile can be made to ministers. Take a minister out west or in some parts of Ontario; he may have several charges and it is imperative that he have an automobile. Some fair allowance should be made on an annual basis without its being necessary for these men to keep the receipts
Income War Tax

they get every time they buy gas or oil. There should also be a reasonable depreciation allowance. An automobile is absolutely necessary in their work and some fair allowance should be granted.

This question has come up in previous sessions. I am not going to press it now, but I want to let the minister know that at some time or another we want some action. There should be not only an allowance not only for automobiles which are needed by ministers to visit their flocks, but be some exemption in regard to the cost of the automobile. This brings to my mind the old question of clergymen of the Protestant religion who are paid so much money as against priests of the Roman Catholic church who do not receive salaries or stipends. Some take the vow of poverty and do not have a fixed income.	At any rate they are not
assessable and I think that point will be granted. Whether a man has a family or whether he is a celibate he has to have a roof over his head. If we are to have equality between the two religions in this country, some consideration should be given to ministers of the Protestant persuasion who must provide themselves with a manse or a lodging of some description. If the church sees fit to give the minister a manse, the rental value must be computed and added to his income and he pays on the total amount.
I am only asking that equality prevail as between the two religions. I think all members of this house believe that we must have equality, no matter what faith one belongs to. I will leave it with the minister at the present time. This is a matter which comes up periodically, although I have not had any letters on it this particular session. But it has come up in previous years, and those of us who belong to the Protestant persuasion believe that equality of treatment should be given to our ministers.
I should like to ask the minister under what section of the income tax act is the wife of a farmer able to carry on a poultry division of her own and not have her income bulked in with the general income of the farm? Is that done under a section of the income tax act?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext:
There is no particular form for that type of return; it just gets down to a matter of practice and regulation where the law does not see the last nickel or the last drop and takes into consideration the peculiar circumstances of the woman on the farm. I just want to make one observation with reference to the remarks the hon. member made

about the taxation of clergymen. As far as income tax returns are concerned, clergymen of all denominations in Canada are dealt with on exactly the same basis.

If the minister had
enough experience in his department-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I have had plenty of experience. I do not propose to let the hon. member for Rosedale broadcast any such statement to the people of Canada as he has done. I know his purpose.
You know my purpose? Apparently the minister is imputing motives, although I do not know just why. If he is imputing motives, I ask him to withdraw.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is nothing to withdraw.
He said, "I know his purpose." What is my'purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Something trivial I would say.
I am asking for equality in this matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is no implication.
The minister said that he thought he knew my purpose. I happened to be handling a matter, a religious matter, that requires a certain amount of delicacy. The minister has made an imputation-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. All that the hon. member needs to do is to state that he has no purpose and the minister must accept his statement.

I will tell the minister what my purpose is. My purpose is to obtain equality. I understand-I may be wrong in this, and I am not suggesting that there is anything wrong with the departmental administration-that there is by reason of circumstances that cannot be changed an inequality in the treatment of housing accommodation which the Protestant clergy have as against that of the Roman Catholic clergy. I do not, from what I know, believe that the Roman Catholic clergy receive stipends in the same way that the Protestant clergy do. Many Roman Catholic clergymen take vows of poverty and therefore cannot have any incomes; yet they must live and have a roof over their heads. There is a disparity there and I ask that consideration be given to it.

Income War Tax
As to the other matter, the minister will find that what I have said after looking into this matter for a long time is a fair statement. I was not trying to raise a difficult issue with him. I think that my statement was quite justified; that the case I put was a reasonable one and that I did not need to be put in my place as the minister tried to do.
I have also asked what particular form the farmer uses in order that his wife may have a separate account for the poultry division of the farm or whatever it may be. The minister says that there is no separate account. I am not suggesting for one moment that the farmer's wife is not entitled' to some return for her services, but in my riding, particularly in one section where there are thousands of small shops, there are many wives who work in the shop during the day in addition to doing all their housework and getting meals for the family, and also work late at night in the shop, particularly at this season of the year. If there is a section of the income tax which allows justice to be done to the farmer's wife who helps her husband I want the same justice to be done to the wives of the -men who live in my riding and who help to swell the total of the storekeepers' earnings, and I ask under what section is this done with regpect to the farmer's wife, or is there some rule or regulation that the ordinary taxpayer does not know about? Let us know what the law of the land is, so that we can tell where we standi. If there is such a section of the act I should like to know about it, and I would feel it incumbent upon me to advise those wives who do work in the store with their husbands that they are entitled to the same treatment as the farmer's wife. I do not want to make it so difficult that it cannot be administered, but I think we must have a certain amount of justice in this matter.
' Mrs. STRUM: I am sorry that I have not heard all this discussion. I should like to ask the minister if a wife who teaches school submits a separate income tax statement from her husband's?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And does he get an exemption for her as his wife?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

And she gets another
exemption as teacher?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Which means that if you teach school you get an edge of 1600 on the woman who helps her husband on the farm or in the store.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know that it is correct to say that you get an edge of that much, but undoubtedly the taxation system is just as the hon. member has described it.

I would ask the minister to give consideration to the question that the hon. member for Rosedale has just raised, because there is no doubt that the wife on the farm has always had an economic value. I know. You start in the morning and wash the separator. It is not possible for your husband to milk the cows, for instance, or to attend to the family garden, or to the whole business of raising chickens, which provides a valuable addition to the nation's food supply. All this depends upon whether the wife is willing to undertake that work. It is in the interest of the production of cream and butter and cheese and chickens that we should give recognition to the wife and allow an additional exemption for the work she does in assisting her farmer husband, and by the same token an exemption should also be allowed for the woman who helps her husband in the store or post office.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This was fully discussed
before the hon. member came in this afternoon and I do not think it is necessary to repeat what I said then. I see no possibility of making a special exemption. It would amount to fixing in the law an allowance by the husband to his wife for the work she does that contributes to his income, and it would be utterly impossible to draw the line anywhere, as far as "I could see, because nearly all wives do work which contributes to the earning of the income by the husband. I do not think we can do anything like that.
The argument-of equity which was raised by the hon. member for Souris, and which he has raised in previous years, was that the wife who leaves the home and goes out and earns money, perhaps making it necessary for someone else to work in the home, is permitted to submit a separate income tax return and nevertheless the husband does not lose his status as a married person. But as I explained to the hon. member this afternoon the reason why this was done in 1942 was that we had to meet an acute and emergent situation as far as workers in war factories were concerned. One can tell what the value of the services of the wife is in that case; it is what she gets
Income War Tax

in cash. In the other case I do not think it would be possible for the law to go to every farm and into every home and store and assess the value of the wife's services to the husband as far as the earning of his income is concerned. We may as well face this fact, that if we make a special concession for one case, we must do it for all.

There is one other point I wish to raise. We have done everything on our side of the house to curtail this debate in order to get on with the business of the house, because we 'realize that this is in a sense a temporary budget, eleven months of the year having gone by and that we shall soon be meeting here again. I wish to ask the minister whether the main provision of the budget, whereby a reduction at the rate of sixteen per cent will be put into effect for the last quarter of this year, representing four per cent for that period, may from the point of view of the department preclude any further tax relief for 1946, if we pass the resolution now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not make it impossible.

No. I know that legally one parliament, or one session of parliament, cannot bind another. We 'do as we want to here. But in the minister's view is this provision of 16 per cent relief from taxation to be the final measure of relief for 1946?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot make predictions about what will be done in the next budget.
I should not be pressed to do that.

I see, according to to-day's paper, that the butter ration may be reduced next year. The little discussion which has taken place here reflects back to the farm wife. I venture to say that a very large proportion of the public do not know how much the farmer's wife contributes ...to the butter production of this country, and in my opinion some way must be found to encourage butter production. Although we have over 100,000 more cattle in Canada than previously, the trend is to lower production, in butter, as well as in hogs, and there is only one reason for it. .When taxation takes away beyond a certain amount of a person's income the taxpayer begins to think that he will not produce any more because the proceeds are going to be taxed away from him. The only way I can see to relieve this condition is to raise the amount of exemption to, say $5,000, and then we shall have a freer flow of goods. But we cannot continue to tax the ability of 
people to produce without having a great curtailment of production all the way down the line.	[DOT]

I wish to thank the minister for the detailed explanation he gave of his law. Sometimes I think we tend to regard our own laws as we regard the law of gravity beyond our control; I do not think that is a legitimate basis on which to argue, because here you have a situation where you are asking someone to undertake production, and am I to understand that we have never made concessions to anybody for the production of certain articles? We have made all kinds of grants in the matter of income tax exemptions, through accelerated depreciation and a number of other devices, in order to get certain jobs done and certain articles produced. Is it suggested that in order to give consideration to the economic contribution which the wife makes on her farm that she and her neighbour change places and they pay each others wives for the work? Not only have farm women produced all kinds of food during the war, but they have helped to build up an industry. It is not a matter of whether a man on a farm can afford a wife; a man on a farm cannot afford to be without a wife. She is the most useful general-purpose labour-saving device there is on the farm.

Where does the husband
come in?

On the basis of the consideration we give to other groups and other industries in order to get certain articles produced, I think it is only just, as an hon. member has suggested, that we raise the exemption, recognizing the need to produce more food and to encourage women to do the thing that they are equipped to do, namely to assist their husbands in producing. I suggest that we review our own law and the basis for it if this is the way it stands at the moment.

I wish to support the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in her argument. I think she gave a very good argument, and I would support it further because I know what it is to try to farm without a wife on the farm.

I should like to ask the minister one brief question before six o'clock, and that is with respect to the exemptions to which professional persons are entitled. Is it true that certain professions are given exemptions from income tax to permit them to pursue post-graduate courses or for the purchase of equipment such as medical kit or books needed in their profession? I have in mind teachers, professors, and so on. I should like an answer covering these two

Dominion-Provincial Conference
cases, the case of persons pursuing postgraduate work, and who may be said to be maintaining the capital equipment with which the professional man operates; and in the second case, expendable equipment, such as the books of the teacher or the medical kit of the doctor.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; the expense of postgraduate work is not allowed. With regard to books and instruments, I do not know. If the outgo is small it is regarded, I think, as an operating expense of carrying on the business rather than a capital expenditure.
The department would rule that this is an expense, of doing the business of the profession, but that the study portion- the sabbatical year study and so on-is not considered an expense?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right. In the case of equipment, instruments and books, they would not be allowed in large sums because that would be a capital expenditure; but there is a small running expenditure which is allowed as an expense.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resolution agreed to.

I should like to thank the hon. member for Qu'Appelle for her kind remarks.
Progress reported.

Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I with the consent of the house, be permitted to make a brief statement.
During the afternoon session of the coordinating committee of the dominion-provincial conference yesterday, I made a statement to the committee on behalf of the government, which I now desire to repeat to the. house. As far as we can now see into the future, it will be necessary to continue for a considerable period certain regulations arising from the war. This period may be a year; it may be less or more than a year.
The war measures relating to collective bargaining and wage control, as part of the price control machinery, are integrated matters. It is government policy to continue these war labour measures until at some future date they can be discontinued without the risk of contributing to inflation. Whatever the date, sufficient notice of the proposed discontinuance of federal administration of measures relating to collective bargaining and wage control will be given to provincial governments
to enable them to take in these fields whatever administrative action they may deem necessary. It was indicated by the representatives of the provinces that they desired to continue to cooperate in the policy as they have during the war.

.22. To provide for an appropriate additional tax dependent on the income of the taxpayer in cases where family allowance payments are received in order to adjust the benefits in respect of dependent children.

I think this resolution
is in a class by itself, because it frankly proposes an increase in a tax. As the proposal stands I think it requires considerable clarification if the committee is to understand it, and I would ask the minister to be good enough to give us an explanation. On reference to the statement the minister made on October 12, as reported at page 1006 of Hansard, as closely as I can follow his remarks on that occasion there is some indication that the amendment proposed is to give effect to the changes in family allowances made by order in council last spring at the time the remainder of the 1944 income tax became payable. However, if one follows the remarks of the minister as they are found at the conclusion of the long paragraph in the second column on page 1007 it is apparent that the new scale of adjustments to be proposed is for 1946, and not for 1945 at all.
In the face of this situation, would the minister be good enough to make a statement to clarify what is proposed here? It seems to me that most people understood that when they received family allowances it was not to cost them something in terms of taxation. But the statement of the minister on October 12 indicates that there is to be a considerable recapture of the amount of the allowances. Would the minister be good enough to clarify this proposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. This resolution will
give effect to the principle approved by the house when the Family Allowances Act was passed, that double benefits should not be given by way of family allowance and income tax credits for the same child. The schedule of rates designed to eliminate this duplication as far as possible has been in use for purposes of tax deductions since the payment of allowances commenced in July, 1945.
The amendment to the law will authorize the payment of final liability under these rates for 1945, and will authorize tables of rates appropriate for use in 1946. The scale for 1946 will be slightly different from that of 1945, because we have tried so far as possible to give effect to the reduction in income tax which will obtain in 1946.

This is a most difficult matter, of course, because it was clearly understood at the time the family allowances bill was introduced by the Prime Minister that persons who are getting a deduction from their income tax in respect of children would not get an additional or duplicate benefit through receipt of family allowances.
But. there are so many different tax values for children, depending upon the income, the number of children above sixteen years of age, and the number of dependents other than children, that it is impossible to make a scientific elimination of duplications. So that after putting an enormous amount of work on the problem of elimination of duplication last spring, we finally decided that the only way we could do it would be to pay family allowances to everybody who applied for them and who had children under sixteen years of age, and then to make an approximate elimination of the duplication.
The way we did it then was to provide that anyone with an income over S3,000 would be obliged, in effect, to pay back family allowances. In other words, it would be of no benefit whatsoever for persons who were in receipt of incomes over $3,000 to apply for family allowances, because the duplication there would be complete. We decided that for those who had incomes of up to $1,200 there would be no attempt to make any recapture at all, and that between $1,200 and $3,000 there would be a graded recapture. Perhaps "recapture" is not the best word in the world to use, but it is an attempt to eliminate the duplication. It is not a tax on family allowances. Rather, it is an adjustment by this method of the. income tax credits, in consideration of the fact that the taxpayer has received family allowances, and it was understood that he was not to get both. It was also understood that he would get the larger of the two in all cases. Approximately speaking, the table we put into effect for the period from July 1, 1945, on, which will be confirmed exactly as it is in the legislation we shall propose for the year 1945, does this.

Mr. Chairman, I feel
slighted. I am the only person eligible to collect, and the minister is not even looking this way.

The table for 1946 will be slightly more generous, in view of the fact that the income tax is reduced. Therefore it may be argued fhat the tax value per child will be reduced for the year 1946. So that the two tables will be placed before the house for its approval. It will not be exact. In
