man}r cases we will not eliminate duplication. The taxpayer will get some benefit. In most *cases he will get more than the larger of the two benefits, but in some cases he may get slightly less. However, it is a pretty close approximation.

I hope I am not too late to discuss a matter which possibly should have been discussed earlier. However, I was not in the house this afternoon, having arrived only this evening. Since this is the last resolution under the Income War Tax Act, I should like to place before the -minister the case of a Toronto gentleman-and I know the minister is familiar with it. This is a man who had been in the United States for some years, and had worked to a point where he was receiving a very good income. Later, however, he decided to return to Canada, and made his return when the year was half over. He received, first, his United States income, and then came back to Canada and earned income here.
' He was taxed in Canada on the income which he made in the United States, and on which he had already paid United States income tax, and then of course he was taxed on the income he made here in Canada. Is the minister familiar with the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
I have forgotten the name.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The name does not make any difference. I am not familiar with the case, but that is the practice which is followed. The gentleman would be taxed on his entire income, but he would be entitled to a credit against his Canadian tax of the United States tax that he had to pay.

I am glad to know that. I shall send him the Hansard for to-day, because the information and figures he sent me' showed that he had to pay in Canada on the whole of his income, and also a second time on the part he got in the United States. He paid two income taxes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the net result he does not pay two income taxes. He is liable for a Canadian tax because he was resident in Canada part of the year. He may also be liable for a United States tax.
He paid that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he paid it, then he is entitled to a credit against the Canadian tax of the amount of the United States tax, provided that the United -States is not higher, and I do not think it would be.

Is it not a waste of time to send out cheques to men whose salaries are more than $2,400? Ia the case of a man with a salary from $2,400 to $2,600, under the present system of deductions he will have to repay seventy per cent of the money he receives.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct.
In the case of a salary between $2,600 and $2,800 it will be eighty per cent, and from $2,800 to $3,000 it will be ninety per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

If a man is employed and his employer is deducting the tax, he is all right, but where a man is not employed it seems to me that there is a good chance of this money not being recovered. Actually you are only lending the man some money because you are going to get practically all of it back. I noticed with some consternation that the cost in postage alone for sending these cheques out for the nine months of the current fiscal year was $500,000, and I suppose there are other expenses. I suppose as far as the government is concerned it is simply taking it out of the one pocket and putting it into the other; I suppose the Post Office Department would benefit from that $500,000, or it might be only a bookkeeping entry, but there is a certain amount of work involved on the part of the postmen and those sending out the cheques. It is not particularly beneficial to the recipient to give him 'money which he will have to pay back when- he might be less able to pay it. As he gets it he is likely to spend it, being human. There are few people who are able to save money. It seems to me that in the case of those in the higher income brackets, where the greater part of the money will be recovered, it is unwise to send out the cheques.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is an administrative problem. The Department of National Health and Welfare are of the opinion that they cannot possibly make deductions from the regular family allowance monthly payments, de-
Income War Tax

pending on the income of the recipient. They do not know what the income is or what it will turn out to be at the end of the year. The only way it can be adjusted is to have it done by the taxing department. As the hon. gentleman has quite properly pointed out, we may lose some of the money. There will be some from whom an amount will not be recovered, but I do not think the loss will be very great, particularly as most people in the country are paying their income taxes currently, either by having them deducted from their pay cheques or by paying in instalments as they go along. An overwhelm^ ing majority of the taxpayers in the country are paying their taxes in that way. The officials all say that this is by far the cheapest and simplest administrative method of eliminating duplication. They say that we should have one simple rule in the Department of National Health and Welfare; that is, to pay family allowances in full to everybody who applies for them and who can qualify. They advise that that be done irrespective of what the income is and then have adjustments made in the taxation.
Does the act provide any means whereby the allowance may be stopped before a child has passed out of the age limit or died?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My recollection is that it provides for the payment to the proper person, to the mother as it is administered, in respect of all children under sixteen years. There is a section, perhaps unnecessary, included to make it clear beyond peradventure that nothing in the act shall prevent an adjustment in tax deduction in respect of the children so as to eliminate duplication,
If a man is earning more than $3,000 a year, could he inform the department and stop the payment of the allowance to his children?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He can withdraw his application for children's allowances; he may refrain from applying.
I know he can refrain from applying, but once the flow has started, is there any way to stop it before the child dies or reaches the age of sixteen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we have infringed on personal liberty to such an extent that we can compel a man to take money that he refuses to take. He has a statutory right to the money which he can waive.
I thought the right was vested in the child with the money being administered by the parents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not vested in the child. The person entitled to the money is the mother, not the child.

I think the minister could give more publicity to that point, because there are many people who do not realize that if their income is over $3,000 they gain nothing by applying for family allowances. As I understand the matter, a person with an income of $2,500 does not gain anything, and I think there would be fewer applications and a great deal of duplication, effort and cost would be avoided if greater publicity were given to this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We published it in every newspaper in Canada, by way of advertisements and in the news columns, and we advertised it over the radio. We did everything we possibly could to inform -the people of Canada last May or June.
Does the minister mean to say that he has publicized the fact that those with incomes of $3,000 or more would not gain by i-t?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We certainly did.

Many of these family allowance cheques are made payable to the mother. Some three or four years ago I had some correspondence with the minister by which I tried to promote the thought that either the wife or the husband should be recognized as the head of the household. I can remember when the income tax exemption was $2,000 for a married man and $1,000 for a single man. Now the exemption is reduced to $660, which puts both the husband and the wife into the single category. Even at this late day I -think the government should- give consideration to -this problem, because there is a tendency to attempt to lower the income of the wife below $660 in order that the husband may again enjoy the benefit of a married man's income tax exemption. This leads to a certain amount of fraud. Trust agreements are entered into whereby certain assets belonging to the wife are turned over to the husband in order to reduce her income below $660. They should be given the right' to decide between themselves who is to be the head of the family. We know that in some houses the wife is the head of the household, but whoever is the head should be entitled to the exemption. I suppose that as a general rule it would be -the ordinary breadwinner of the home, the husband, but he should have the exemption that a married man would enjoy. Then the wife could be taxed as a single person. What happens now is that these allowances are paid to the mother.

Excess Profits Tax
How are you going to account for that? A woman may -have two or three children, but the amount paid to her in the form of family allowances will not be enough to make her income taxable and1 the government will lose, even though the husband may be earning a taxable income. I should like the minister to explain how they propose to offset the cheques that are payable to the mother, who, we will assume, has no earned income. Therefore she will receive the family allowance while her husband has an income that will be taxed. What becomes of the income in a case of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The family' allowance is not taxable. It. is exempt from taxation by statute. The husband is taxed on his income, and in the higher income categories he is taxed more than he otherwise would be by virtue of the fact that the wife gets the family allowance income. That is proper, because the receipt of the family allowance reduces the dependency of the child on the father, and therefore he should not have the same tax deduction with respect to that child that he otherwise would have. That is what is meant by the elimination of duplication of benefits.
If the cheque goes to the home, do I understand that the husband when making his return has to state whether or not the family allowance was received on account of the child?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right,

I would like the minister to believe that I am helping him because the minister of health goes around spreading happiness by issuing these cheques and then another minister spreads gloom by taking the money back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hardly agree.

That, is why I want the minister to understand that I am working hard for him. I think it is possible on the part of the government to avoid this trouble as they have a formula whereby they can prevent the sending out of the cheques, because a statement has been sent out to employers showing how much they must deduct from the wages of their workmen. The same statement could be used by the Department of Health in reducing the amount of the cheque. It is simple enough when you go at it in the right way. The employer gets it back, but unfortunately the Minister of Health does not know and does not want to know and does not want to hold it back. I should like to prevent the sending of the cheque and then the enforced recovery, and
I suggest that the Minister of Finance take the matter up with the Minister of Health and make a more equitable distribution of the joys and sorrows of office.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Resolution agreed to.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolved that it is expedient to amend the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, and to provide:
1.	That individuals and partnerships he exempt from the 15 per cent tax on total profits of 1946.

In his budget address the Minister of Finance said that he would make no statement on the taxation of cooperatives until after the commission's report had been tabled. Since the report has now been tabled, would the minister state whether the government has reached a decision as to the taxation of. cooperatives this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The government has not yet made a decision. It will be impossible to do it in this budget, and whether we do it by separate legislation or not I doubt whether we shall be able to do it this session.
You will not be using the emergency powers act to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It is not likely to be done this session?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not likely to be. It may be; there is nq decision by the government. If there is a decision to do something it will have to be made very soon. But present probabilities are that that question will not 'be tackled this session.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
2.	That the tax on excess profits of indirfiduals and partnerships in 1946 be reduced from 100 per cent of the excess profits to 60 per cent of that portion of the excess profits which are in excess of 117-647 per cent of the standard profits, and that the provision for refund of a portion of the tax be repealed.

A statement might be made" here by the Minister of Finance by way of correction of an impression that has gone abroad as a result of some emphasis that was put in the budget speech and in press comments on the proposed reduction in the excess profits tax. The thought that went abroad was that there was to be in place of the 100 per cent less twenty per cent excess profits tax a straight sixty per cent. But actually what is proposed is sixty per cent, plus a formula based on a breaking point. I suggest that to the average taxpayer "breaking point" is represented by the present scale of
Excess Profits Tax

taxation, but for the purposes of this resolution the breaking point has to do with these figures with reference to standard profits; namely, in the case of individuals and partnerships 117-647 per cent of the standard profits; in the case of corporations and joint stock companies which have filed consolidated returns, 117-241 per cent of the standard profits; and in the case of other corporations and joint stock companies 116-667 per cent of the standard profits. When you come to apply this formula to the-calculation of the excess profits tax that will be payable, the minister will agree that you do not get a uniform excess profits tax of sixty per cent based on the present rate. I have some calculations before me which show that it would result as follows:
If the reduction were calculated on the present- tax structure and the sixty per cent tax were applied without the introduction of this new formula with the breaking point, there would be a lower tax than the resolution proposes on companies having profits between 116-66 per cent and 155-55 per cent of standard profits.' Similarly, where there are excess profits of 155-55 per cent of standard profits, the present proposals would work out the same as sixty per cent on the old basis without the new formula. Similarly, corporations with excess profits of more than 155-55 per cent of standard profits will actually pay less than the sixty per cent would amount to apart from the application of the formula. In view of the impression that has gone abroad that the new proposals call for a straight sixty per cent excess profits tax calculated, on the old basis, it is desirable that the minister make a statement clarifying the position because that is not the way it is going to work out. There will be variations depending upon the application of the formula to the amount of excess profits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Under the present law sole proprietors and partnerships are required to pay an excess profits tax equal to the greater of either fifteen per cent of total profits or 100 per cent of excess profits. The practical effect, of this provision is that when total profits are less than 117-647 per cent of standard profits the fifteen per cent rate on total profits applies, but when total profits exceed 117-647 per cent of standard profits the 100 per cent rate on excess profits applies, since this gives a tax greater than fifteen per cent of total profits above this point.
It is proposed by these two resolutions that the fifteen per cent rate be repealed and that a rate of sixty per cent be 'levied on profits in excess of 117-647 per cent of standard profits

in place of the present rate of 100 per cent. It will be recalled that twenty per cent of the 100,per cent rate now payable on profits in excess of 117-647 per cent of standard is refundable to the taxpayer after the war. In reducing the rate to sixty per cent the requirement of paying this refundable portion has been dropped and, in addition, another twenty per cent of the 100 per cent rate has been removed, leaving a net rate of sixty per cent.
In consequence of this change no sole proprietor or partnership will pay any excess profits tax on 1946 income if such income falls below 117-647 per cent of its standard profits, and will pay a rate of sixty per cent of its profits in excess of 117-647 per cent of its standard profits if its total profits come above this point.
Is that the explanation the hon. gentleman
desires?

My point goes beyond that. It is the effect of the application of this formula in regard to the breaking point on corporations. Take the various classes, those whose excess profits happen to be on the breaking point, those below, and those above, because it does not work out at a uniform basis of sixty per cent on the present tax basis. I am speaking now of the impression which has gone abroad about the effect of the proposed reductions. It is not simply a reduction to sixty per cent based on the present calculation; there has been introduced a new formula with a breaking point which has to be taken into account. That is my point.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that nearly all business men, certainly all chartered accountants in the country, and a great many lawyers, understand this breaking point. The provisions regarding excess profits tax-I am speaking now about excess profits tax on corporations, because that is the case which ordinarily occurs-
That is what I was speaking of, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
After you go all through the complicated provisions of the excess profits tax the method of computation is fairly simple. A company is taxed forty per cent on its profits up to 116 2/3 per cent of its standard profits and it is taxed 100 per cent on its profits in excess of 116-2/3 of its standard profits. That is the breaking point. That leaves a company seventy per cent of its standard profits; because forty per cent of 116 2/3 per cent is 46 2/3, which, subtracted from 116 2/3, leaves 70. So that the formulae and alternatives and options and cross-refer-

Excess Profits Tax
encea and so forth all come to this: you just tell me what the profits of a company are in terms of its standard profits; that is, if you tell me that the profits of this company were 150 per cent of its standard profits, I can reckon the income and excess profits tax for you in ten minutes.
Liberally speaking!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I take forty per cent of 116 2/3 of its standard profits and set that down there, and then 100 per cent of the difference between 116 2/3 and 150 per cent. It is that 100 per cent which has been reduced to sixty per cent by this budget; there is a variation for companies submitting consolidated returns, and there is a variation for partnerships and sole proprietors; but the breaking point in the case of partnerships and sole proprietors is 116-666, and 117-647 is the breaking point for companies submitting consolidated returns-not 116-666 but 117-241. But the principle is clear that what was 100, the 100 per cent above the breaking point, has been reduced to sixty. When I say "100," it is fair to say "80" of course, because twenty per cent of the 100 per cent is returnable.

I think I should say at the outset that the government is to be commended for having made an effort, to provide something which should lend considerable incentive to our recovery in the post-war period. I personally would have been very glad if the time had arrived when we could do away with the excess profits tax, because I believe that private enterprise, given the green light, will play a greater part in the solution of our post-war problems than we can ever hope to do by direction in this chamber. The minister has said that many lawyers understand the breaking point. I am informed that there is no excess profits tax on lawyers, so that they probably would be the first to recognize the breaking point since it does not involve any of their profits-if they could be determined. I hear someone nearby say that they have no profits.
It is all profit.

The lawyers whom it is my privilege-I use that word so that I shall be understood-to know, look to be fairly well fed. Therefore I think they are doing fairly well in seeking to intrepret the statutes and the laws which this government has put upon the statute books. The only thing which keeps lawyers in business is trying to interpret the law. I read from this section that there will be a tax of 60 per cent on that portion of the excess profits which are in excess of 117-647 per cent of the standard
profits, and that the provision for refund of a portion of the tax is repealed. My question is, will there be no longer any refund to corporations, even though they are subject to a certain portion of the tax as explained by the minister; if they go above this amount they are subject to the 100 per cent tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
That is, if they go above a ,certain amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right; they are subject to 60 per cent of the excess above the breaking point, with no refund.
There will be no refund?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

I think the barristers and solicitors of Canada are remiss in not tendering a hearty vote of thanks to the Minister of Finance for the stupendous continuous income he has been providing for them. The public cannot understand the income tax law. The lawyers cannot either, but they are privileged to charge for interpreting it, and I think the lawyers should have tendered the minister and his department a hearty vote of thanks.	,	.

Let us give it to
them now.

Up to March 31 of this year the government had collected $184,500,000 of refundable excess profits tax. That is to be given back to the corporations in the next two or three years. I should like to know if any policy has been formulated as to what the corporations will be allowed to do with this refund tax. Will they be allowed to use it for dividends or for capital purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is their money; they can do as they like with it.
They can use it for dividends?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, for any purpose they wish. That was clearly understood from the beginning. That question was faced and settled in 1941 or 1942. The question was, whether this would be tied up and restrictions placed upon its use or whether it would be regarded as the money of the taxpayer, and I decided that the proper policy was to regard it as the money of the taxpayer. It must be borne in mind that when you have a 100 per cent tax, even if it is refundable, you have put into operation forces which make for extravagance, for inefficiency, for lack of effort, and so on, and you must be careful not to go
Excess Profits Tax

too far, otherwise you will hurt your national efficiency considerably. I felt that the point to stop was where we did stop. That is, we take the 20 per cent and keep it, we have not paid any interest on it, and have retained it for quite a long time. When the time comes for them to get it back, it i3 theirs.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.
3.	That for 1946 the following rates of tax apply to corporations:
(a)	Twenty-two per cent of the profits of corporations and joint stock companies before deduction therefrom of any tax paid thereon under the Income War Tax Act;
(b)	In the case of corporations and joint stock companies which have filed consolidated returns, 20 per cent, of the profits which are in excess of 117-241 per cent of the standard profits of such consolidated companies;
(c)	In the case of other corporations and joint stock companies 20 per cent of the profits which are in excess of 116-66 per cent of the standard profits.
and that the provision for refund of a portion of the tax be repealed.	.
Resolution agreed to.
4.	That on the profits of 1946 and subsequent years the minimum standard profits of taxpayers be increased from $5,000 to $15,000, and that where a taxpayer's standard profits are oh January 1. 1946, in excess of $5,000 but less than $25,-000 they be increased by one-half the difference between their present amount and $25,000.
Resolution agreed to.
5.	That the special rate of tax applicable to businesses commencing after June 24, 1944, not apply to cases where in the opinion of the minister there has been no bona fide commencement of a new or substantially different business.
Will the minister explain this resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To provide greater certainty for new businesses in their first year of operation, the Excess Profits Tax Act was amended in 1944 to limit the tax payable under that act on income of the first year to the minimum rate of twenty-two per cent, because of the danger that existing businesses might take on the guise of a new business by simply reorganizing and acquiring a new legal identity without any real change in either the ownership or the type of business conducted. It is proposed that the Minister of National Revenue must be satisfied that the business is either an entirely new business or a substantially different business before allowing a claim to be taxed under the minimum rate on these grounds.

I suggest to the minister that that is a drastic provision and one which should be given further consideration.
Take the case of a man who is carrying on business in his own name without being incor-
porated. In good faith he forms a company, and lias been carrying on for the last eighteen months as an incorporated company. I believe in many, many cases that was done without the slightest sign of bad faith; that the men who did it were advised by responsible advisers, and even by income tax officers, that they were eligible for this lower tax. They have conducted' their business for eighteen months on that understanding, and now they are faced with the possibility of an amendment under which other officials of the department can step in and say this was not a change made in good faith; that it was made to cut down the rate of taxation, and that therefore they are liable for the heavier tax. That would be done^ after these men have made their plans in perfectly good faith. I should like to put that before the minister. I know of cases of that kind, and I do not think it is wise for the government to step in now and say that they must show that the change was not made in bad faith.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not looked the matter up, but I think all the explanations of the changes that were mkde were on this basis, that when people want to go into new businesses they have no experience of earnings and it is impossible to get a standard profit fixed; they do not know what their rate of taxation is to be, or they do not know what their standard profit is because they are starting something new. That was the; reason for the change in the law; it was not that some person might change the form of his business. Take, for example, a business that was paying heavily under the excess profits tax; it was incorporated and called a new business. The tax was pulled down to forty per cent. That was not the intention or the real meaning of the law, and it was never put forward on those grounds; it was put forward to meet a particular situation. I do not think they ought to be allowed to get away with it.

An officer of the Department of National Revenue has interpreted the provision that was passed last year as meaning in some cases that if a person incorporated his business, changed his business in the normal way to meet business growth, he would be entitled to the benefit of that section. It would not be so bad if the provision applied to those where bad faith could be shown, that they made the alteration to benefit by the tax, but that is not the way it is worded. It makes every person who has benefited, by the provision show that there has been good faith; in other words, it puts everybody under suspicion who has made a change of that kind

Excess Profits Tax
I think very serious damage will be done, particularly to younger men who in the normal course have built up a business and reached the stage where they had to incorporate; and have done so believing that they were entitled to the benefits of this act. In the long run the government would benefit from that change to a corporation because the company will be liable to tax bn its profits and shareholders to tax on their dividends. I know there are cases where "there has not been the slightest bit of bad faith where they will be absolutely crippled by this new provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall give consideration to the hon. gentleman's representations before the bill is prepared ; but in saying that I do not know whether I shall do what he has requested, because I must say that when we bring in a bill to meet a specific need and everybody understands it, I do not like to see people, just because they are clever and the law will permit it, reduce their taxes as a result of that. Perhaps this retroactive legislation is not good on general principles, but I have sponsored some of it once in a while in order to prevent people from getting away with too much. I do not know whether that is the case here or not, but perhaps there has been some taking advantage of what is the letter of the law without any regard for the spirit of it.

This is retroactive legislation not for a period of six months but for a period of eighteen months. I think the minister will agree with me 'that the great majority of Canadian business men are not dishonest; they want to pay their just .debts. This excess profits taxation and income taxation are now so complicated that the ordinary business man has to depend on his accountant, his auditor or the income tax officers themselves for advice. I know of cases where they received advice on that basis, are entirely innocent, and now are caught by this amendment.
The hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned corporations under this resolution. Does this resolution apply equally to partnerships and* sole ownerships?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon, gentleman asking if it applies to a partnership which converts itself into a company?
A simple partnership, not incorporated, or to come down to a more simple case, a sole ownership.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It must be a new business.
Yes, it would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, it applies not only to corporations but to any person-and "person" would include a corporation'-who has commenced business after the 26th day of June, 1944, or carries on a substantially different business to which subsection 4 of section 5 of the act is applicable, and uses therein physical assets substantially different from those he used in the business previously carried on.

Take a sole ownership business. During the course of the last four, five or six years a certain amount has been set up as a reserve as a result of the twenty per cent refundable portion. A bank or lending institution, knowing that at some time or another this amount will be refunded to the owner of this business, lends the owner perhaps $30,000 or $40,000 with which he puts up a new building as an addition to his present 'business. Will he come under this special provision?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he carries on a substantially different business.
What is meant by "substantially different"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he carries on a substantially different business to which subsection 4 of section 5 of this act is applicable, and uses therein physical assets substantially different from those he used in the business he previously carried on, then his standard profits are limited. It is a forty per cent rate he pays if it is a corporation, and fifteen per cent if it is an individual or sole proprietorship. There is no difficulty about that provision in regard to carrying on a substantially different business and using'therein physical assets. That is not a difficult thing to determine; there is no trouble about it. The difficulty is in regard to the first part of it, a taxpayer who has commenced business after the 26th day of June, 1944.
That is a new business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Then let me place before the minister what might be a definite case. Take a boot and shoe man on Bank street here in Ottawa. He has accumulated a fairly large reserve. Just around the corner a shoe repair establishment has made considerable progress, and he feels that he would like to enter into the business of repairing shoes and manufacturing special types of shoes. He uses his reserve. Does he come under section 5, since he is using part of the capital of his business; or will it be considered a new establishment?
Excess Profits Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hesitate to give a ruling on a set of facts. A ruling on the exact facts of the case would have to be obtained from the Department of National Revenue.

That is what you want those in retail business to do; you want them to reinvest their money with a view to providing greater employment. I think it is definitely understood and agreed that during the last four or five years the retail business man has been kept down to a certain limit as far as profits are concerned. He has not been permitted to make more than a certain standard profit. His 100 per cent excess has been taken away from him. notwithstanding the fact that ' his bills receivable have grown, his stocks have grown, and he has not had the necessary capital to work with. He has accumulated a certain amount which is refundable, and he wishes to invest that money in an establishment such as I have mentioned. The funds have been earned by his established business. Will you charge him under this new section 5?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the new investment and the acquisition of different assets are of sufficient importance and extent, so that, a reasonable man would say he is embarking upon a substantially different business, then he would be entitled to the advantages of this section.
Take the case I mentioned, which is closely identified with the established business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With the same old business?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the national revenue department I understand they have a committee which has precedents and some principles upon which they work, but I do not see how I can rule on that. I do not see how I can go any farther than I have gone. There are the principles.
Hire a lawyer.

We should not have to hire lawyers. I do not wish to pursue this further, but I would point out that if you expect business men to reinvest funds in new business which will give added employment, then I believe that within the very near future you should settle that question and say yes or no; or give them the green light and
lMr. Isnor.]
say they may carry on and they will be taxed no more than the regular business is taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Any person interested in such a venture can get a yes or no from the Department of National Revenue on submitting all the facts to them, but I cannot go any farther than to state the principles that apply.	,

I was pleased to hear the minister say in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South that he would give some further consideration to this resolution. He did say that he hesitated to change that which was already written, and I can understand that because I believe there were some repercussions from certain proposed changes in the tariff schedules which were introduced in the budget speech. Yesterday we heard the Minister of Public Works say that his figures and estimates were prepared before the war was ended, and that they did not include post-war plans. I should like the minister to say whether the figures in these various resolutions have been revised since the conclusion of the war. For instance, I cannot imagine resolution 5 being included in the budget if the war were still in progress. This is a partial post-war budget; is that right? The minister is the man who takes all the abuse for the government, and I believe he has done a very fine job. The other ministers say they have not made any post-war plans, but apparently the Minister of Finance has been alive to the situation and has made certain definite proposals to encourage post-war business. So that he recognizes, whether or not the other ministers do, that the war is over and this is partly a post-war budget. [DOT]

Would it not be fair to make this provision apply from the date of the budget? There was legislation passed last year, and under that legislation people had certain rights. As I said before, I believe that in some cases they were actually told by the department that they could do this or could do that. Why should their rights not be based entirely upon the legislation of last year? Why should it be necessary now to bring in a provision which not only will cover the future, but contains a punitive quality, and gives the minister power to go back eighteen months and assess taxes against somebody who has been acting on the basis of last year's legislation? What objection would there be to making this provision apply from the date of the budget on, rather than carrying it back to last year?

Excess Profits Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, you just permit situations like this to go unremedied. Men are in partnership and perhaps are paying excess profits taxes, because they are making very high war profits. They come along and read the budget. They read the Excess Profits Tax Act as amended in 1944, and they find out that if they commence business, or if anyone commences business after June 26, 1944, he can obtain a decided advantage, because he does not have to pay any excess profits tax, in the ordinarily accepted sense of the term. He is limited to the regular profits, forty per cent.
So they say, "That is fine. I will incorporate myself, and automatically in the eyes of the law I can be commencing business. In the eyes of the law I shall not have been in business before, because the company was not born. It was not in existence. The life of the company will date from this date." So that in this way he obtains a big tax advantage.
Then, perhaps two partners who are in the same class, as far as excess profits taxes are concerned, will take in an employee, or some other person, with the result that we have a new partnership and the commencement of a new business. Even though the physical assets are the same, even though there is no difference in the type of business, and even though the customers are the same and the operations are the same, and although they should have known or in fact did know, from explanations given, that that was never intended to apply to such a case at all, they form the new company. This was intended for people who were really starting something new, who were commencing a new business, from the ground up. And because you do not have any experience, you have to have a statutory fixation of standard profits. That is the reason this was put in.
It is just a question how far we should go in avoiding retroactive legislation. It looks very much to me like taking advantage of legislation by persons who know that the whole spirit and intent of the legislation was different.
It will be said, "Oh, well, that is your fault. If you bungled your phraseology, if your lawyers were not good enough, and if there was a hole there that people rushed through, you have to let them go through." That is what will be said. But what inequity is there in saying that they must have really commenced a new business on June 26?

The inequity is this, that
while there may have been, a few people who took advantage of that situation, and rushed through the hole, I suggest to the minister that for everyone who did so there were fifty whcwere advised that this was the proper thing to do, who went ahead and laid their plans and made their expenditures on that basis. And they were strictly within their legal rights in doing so. Now the crown comes along and upsets all those legal rights. It goes back eighteen months and says, "We are going to take more tax."
I will point out to the minister the amendment which was put through last year, as it appears in chapter 38 of the statutes:
Provided further that where a person, other than a controlled company described by section fifteen A of this act, in the opinion of the minister	_
(i)	has commenced business after the twentysixth day of June, nineteen hundred and forty-four or	.	.	.
(ii)	carries on a substantially different business to which subsection four of section five of this act is applicable and uses therein physical assets substantially different from those he used in the business he previously carried on.
There the power is entirely "in the opinion of the minister." Somebody in the Department of National Revenue headquarters in Ottawa has made the decision for the minister; somebody decides what the opinion of the minister is in each of these cases. These people have been told that they come under this section.
Now the crown wishes to have new legislation passed which means that the _minister's officials will be allowed to change their minds again, and go back to collect the difference in the tax. I suggest that this is entirely out of line with the whole principle of British justice.
Hear, hear.

It is contrary to British justice, to say nothing of the disastrous effect it may have on business, and just at a time when we are trying to encourage business to go ahead and open up, so that they can hire more people. Here we are, with unemployment becoming a terrible scourge again in my own city of Vancouver. Something drastic must be done or there will be thousands of Canadians unemployed. This government is depending upon private business to furnish most of the employment-and I think quite rightly so. But when you bring in a punitive measure such as this resolution, which is intended to have a retroactive effect, you undermine the confidence of businessmen in the government. I suggest to the minister that further consideration should be given to this resolution before such a drastic step is taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the resolution carries we can back away from it in the act. That is, it is not a case where you are going beydnd anything. I think the resolution ought to be
Excess Profits Tax

allowed t<? pass, and I will give consideration in the act. That is, if the act is more lenient, it does not violate any constitutional principle; if it is more harsh, it would.
We could go on arguing about this for some time. Of course if these firms had taken on more men and had -done a substantially different business there would be no trouble about it at all. But if by just putting on a new shell they seek to get a tax advantage, I do not know that we we under any obligation to help' them out.

I do not think that would apply to the majority of cases. But even if that were so, even if they took advantage of a statute which was poorly drawn last year, there is no reason why the crown should come here to-night and try to go back eighteen months to change that statute. It is purely punitive, and I repeat that such procedure is entirely out of line with the principles of British justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But it does eliminate discrimination between these and other companies. Here is a company which has not been as smart; they have not consulted as good a lawyer, and have not found out about this thing. This company goes on in the same way, and pays its heavy excess profits tax. Surely there is some equity as between that company and another of the kind I described before.
I am willing to consider any safeguard to see that real cases of new businesses get full benefit of the section. But I think it is quite all right retroactively to take that benefit away from people who simply took advantage of the section, who did not commence any new business at all, who did not change their business at all, but who just changed the form of their business for the sake of getting rid of taxation, at a time when other people who did not have the advantage of that type of legal advice and who did not do it kept on paying their higher taxes.
The minister is talking about equities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The minister has no right to interpret legislation once it has been passed; when legislation has been passed, it should be interpreted by the courts. No minister of the crown has the right to come back next year and in order to correct legislation of the year before bring in a new provision that enables him to go back and take money away from people. ' This house laid down the law last year and under that law people did certain 
things which they were entitled to do. If the law was wrong, that was not their fault. The minister has no right to come along now and, in effect, pass a law in November, 1945, to have effect in June, 1944, which alters completely the law that was passed in June, 1944. I think the minister as a very able lawyer will realize the strength of that argument. I suggest to him that this new provision be made applicable from the date of the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will give consideration to that. I do not want any one to think I am trying to interpret the law.
That is what it amounts to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no more authority than any other citizen of this country to put an authoritative interpretation on any statute. The courts are the only authority having the right to do that. I have no authority whatever to change a law and I am not proposing to change this law.
You are, in effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am placing it before
parliament; parliament is the only authority that can change this law.
One minute ago you said only the courts could do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is no use arguing-
It is no use arguing when you have no argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I said that the courts were the only ones that could place an authoritative interpretation on a' statute, and I said that parliament is the only body that can change the law. I do not know what the hon. member for Vancouver South is intimating when he says that I am claiming to have the right to interpret a statute or to change the law.
The minister did not put that quite correctly. In effect that is what he is doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not. ,

This house passed a law last year and people have acted under that law. They have not been held to be without the law. Actually their position is stronger because it is based on the opinion of the minister under the section that was passed last year. Now the minister says this evening, "Oh, well, this did not turn out the way we thought it was going to; there are equities this way and equities that way, and it is only justice that if this man gets caught, this other man should not be allowed a lower tax.

Excess Profits Tax
because the other man did not know anything about it; therefore we are going to start all over again; we are going to remedy this whole thing; we are going to go back to last June with a new law by passing at the present session a law that enables us to review all these cases." I say in effect that puts the minister in the position of interpreting the law rather than leaving it to the courts. I consider it unsound legislation, because it offends against the principle that once a person's rights are determined and he has acted on those rights, there shall be no going back; there shall be no changing the law to upset his position. I would ask the minister to review this carefully and give consideration to the suggestion I have made this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I certainly will do that. If my hon. friend has in mind, any specific cases I should like to examine those bona fide cases he is talking about and see what they look like. I do not know whether they are good or bad'. If they are good, we have no right to touch them. If they are bad, I think we have., However, I will give consideration to the matter.
That simply proves that the minister is interpreting the law. He wants to see these cases and, if he decides that they are good, then he will do something about them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot do anything about them.

That should not be the minister's position at all; he should stand or fall on the law that was passed last year. If the law needs to be amended, let us amend it now by all means but do not make the new law retroactive. Let us start out from now with the new law.

This section 5 is just another example of what we find shot all through the present Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act-more discretion to the minister. I do not think we could have a clearer case than what is set out in the minister's own words. Every businessman must 'bring his tax problem to Ottawa in order to have it decided. This parliament is not passing laws which are capable of decisions so that a business man knows where he stands. No matter how perfect the minister seeks to be in his legislation, I do not think he is ever going to get every person who seeks, by means of a smart lawyer or otherwise, to slip through the net occasionally. If he tightens his taxation net so that not even a sardine can get through the meshes,
he will so hamstring business and create uncertainty that businessmen will not be able to go ahead and provide the goods and services to create employment that they must do if we are to have continued prosperity in this country. *
Let us look at this resolution. First of all, it offends against the sound principle^ of British justice and sound taxation policy in that it is retroactive. It is true there may be a few cases, but the minister has not told the committee how flagrant the violations haye been. Perhaps there are half a dozen cases, but I have no means of knowing or guessing what the element of tax evasion is or how extensive it may be. He might at least tell the committee that there have been scores of cases or hundreds of cases whereby the treasury is going to be out hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars. Let us have some conception of what this is about. Does the minister happen to know of five or six cases across the whole of Canada during the past year and a half where clever lawyers have been able to get around this section and do the treasury out of a few thousand dollars?
In order to collect those few thousand dollars he wants to tighten this section and make it retroactive. He is going to cause uncertainty so that businessmen will not know where they stand. A businessman may have thought he was doing a nice job in building up a new business and creating employment, and now he finds he has another five or ten thousand dollars of taxation to pay which he did not know about. He has to provide for that, and therefore he cannot open up the addition to his business he was planning on opening, or carry out other plans he had1 in mind. He just cannot do that with this uncertain taxation measure hanging over him. A% I say, the retroactive feature is the first offence.
The second dereliction in the resolution is to be found in the phrase "in the opinion of the minister." I do not know how many times that phrase is to be found in the Income War Tax Act and the Excess Profits Tax Act, but it has been estimated that the number is from fifty to 150 times or more. You must come to Ottawa and more often than not make a deal with the tax department because ther^ is no absolute ruling on the subject. They look at your case through their own glasses and no one else can decide for the businessman. No one in Vancouver, for example, can give a decision, much less the businessman himself. Is it any wonder that in the other place they have set up a committee to look into the working and the application of these tax laws? There is no
Excess Profits Tax

greater or more crying need for the good of the business community of this country than a sound revision of the whole income tax law and its administration. People do not know where they stand. I had a case in connection with annuities which I shall certainly refer to later because I have further evidence. No one knows where he stands to-day. We must have some certainty. We cannot go on and create new industry and create jobs unless businessmen know where they stand. I would appeal to the minister not to try to make these laws quite so perfect but to try to realize that business and the creation of jobs constitute the main thing in this country to-day and not to make our tax laws so tight that the shrewdest Al. Capone could not find his way through them, for the businessman is fundamentally honest and is willing to pay taxes, but he must have certainty if he is to go ahead.
This resolution applies particularly to new ' business. If we need anything in this country it is to have new businesses and new industries created. The present economic outlook, to my humble way of thinking, is fraught with just as many uncertainties and just as much hope, hope based on a sounder foundation I trust, than was the expectation in 1929 when we thought we were in a new era and companies were capitalized not on the basis of 1929 earnings but on the basis of what they would be in 1932. We have just come through a great period of progress and industrial expansion in this country in which the national income has doubled and trebled. We have passed laws in this house such as the family allowance, in favour of which we were unanimous to a man, involving an outlay of $250,000,000 a year as compared with a prewar annual budget of $500,000,000. Where ape we to get the money? We are expecting to have a volume of business similar to that pertaining to the war years. That is the hope, and we can put every ounce of strength we have into the realization of that hope because, if we do not do so, the country-I can use very strong words-certainly has a very sorry outlook. We must have a great national income to get the revenue required to carry all the new social measures and to service the debt which we have to-day. We are bound to do so if we possibly can, and we shall have to resort to unusual measures in our endeavour.
This government has a mandate from the people of this country, as was so well put by the hon. member for Cariboo the other night when he said that this government had a mandate from the people to carry on under the banner of private enterprise. If we are to

give private enterprise it's head we must give businessmen some certainty where they stand in the matter of taxation. New business must also be created in order that we may develop our export markets, and that leads me to the whole matter of excess profits taxes.
In the present budget the minister has reduced the effective rate from eighty to sixty per cent. What do we find is being done by our cousins across the line? There, with a much stronger economy than we have, one that is based on domestic business to a far greater extent than Canada's can ever be because we are to a large extent an export country, they have made their excess profits tax nothing at all-no rate-they have abandoned the whole thing as of next January. We in this country must face competition with industries in the United States, particularly in the export field, and while this reduction from an eighty per cent effective rate to sixty per cent is undoubtedly a help, and, I trust, a straw in the wind, I hope that the Minister of Finance will undertake at the earliest opportunity to make further reductions and do away with the excess profits tax which he himself has said leads to the stifling of business, gross carelessness and lack of efficient management.	*
Furthermore, may I say in connection with the effect of this taxation on new business, if we in this country are ever going to meet the challenge which this government has firmly saddled upon it to keep our people in jobs and prosperity, we must have more business. Where it is all going to come from, I do not know. But I know that all check-reins and stifling measures must be taken off our people if we are to begin to have a national income corresponding in any degree with that which we have had in the last three or four years. If we are to attract capital to this country from outside, and we need it badly, not the actual dollars but venturesome money, because there are very few wealthy Canadians among us who can take the chances necessary for the development of our natural resources or the setting up of new businesses, because so many fall by the wayside that very few can really afford to put up any substantial amounts for they must be careful and look after their old age- if we are to attract capital to this country we must have some certainty about our taxation laws.
Furthermore, in regard to this excess profits tax and the results that we now have under immediate discussion, if a company is to extend its business the most likely place where it will find its capital is out of its tax-paid earnings which it ploughs back into the industry. If the rate of taxation is so high

Excess Profits Tax
that there is nothing left, if it is sixty per cent as now on any company with earnings above the 1936-1939 level, it is not going to be able to find earnings with which to expand and create more employment. Therefore I would suggest that this resolution be either dropped entirely or taken back for redrafting, particularly two features, namely, the retroactive feature and the discretionary power given to the minister, which is something we are trying to get away from. Surely we in this house can take adequate time to frame taxation provisions which will become the law' of the land and will not necessitate for their interpretation, as my colleague said a little while ago, everybody flying down or coming down to Ottawa on the trains, and making Ottawa the centre of all their -activities because they do not know where they stand until they get a ruling from the minister. Surely there should be some person in this country other than the minister who can interpret the taxation laws under which business must operate, and under which new businesses coming in must find their roots.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Did the hon. member ever hear of the courts?
The minister has not apparently.

I wish I had heard that ten times as often as I have heard it here. People must come here to Otttawa to see the Minister of National Revenue and his department to find out where they stand under the taxation laws of this country, and if an appeal is taken from a ruling the appeal once ag^in goes back to the minister and his assistants. We do not expect the minister to know all about the peculiar workings of every business in Canada. He must of necessity rely a great deal on his full-time veteran assistants, so that there is virtually no appeal from a ruling on taxation as there is in Great Britain and in the United States. The tax law is made by one set of officials, and the only appeal is to the same set of officials. There is no certainty about the law. It is in the discretion of the minister. Surely we should from this date forward never again pass any section of an income tax or excess profits tax law which cannot be interpreted and the rights under it determined bj' any of the divisional staffs throughout Canada, without having to go to one man and leave it to his discretion as to whether or not one is within or without the terms of the statute.

I should like to give such approval as I may to the argument made by the hon. member for Vancouver South. He 47696-175
might have added to his reasons the importance of maintaining the good reputation of the department.
If a taxpayer has taken a position which was tenable under the statute, it behooves the department to see that the taxpayer's position is maintained. I suggest to the minister that nothing will tend more to shatter the confidence of business in his department and its administration than a changing departmental position and a going back on what the taxpayer thought was the department's plighted word. Questions have to be determined by somebody. Somebody's discretion must settle disputes between people, be they between taxpayers and tax gatherers, or be they in an -unhappy menage. But I am not certain that it is wise to leave an unbounded discretion to an administrative officer, I will attempt to point out what I mean, by reading- resolution 5. Incidentally there appears to be a word or two left out of it. I do not know whether in the minister's text the word "shall" or "does" is left out before the words "not apply". I would be glad of that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I may answer that, the general scheme of the phraseology does not seem to call for a verb there. For instance, in resolution 3 the resolution is "That for 1946 the following rates of tax apply to corporations"; and this is, "That the special rate . . . not apply."

It reads:
5. That the special rate of tax applicable to businesses commencing after June 24, 1944, not apply to cases where in the opinion of the minister there has been no bona nde commencement of a new or substantially different business.
This is "bureaucrese" in English.
Is the text complete?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be better to have "do" in there, or "shall". But apparently the scheme is-

What I 'wanted to come to is this. The minister has this resolution before him; it gives him wide powers of discretion; in a given case he will determine whether or not there has been a "bona fide commencement of a new. or substantially new business." What are the elements of novelty and where are , they located? Are they restricted to the enterprise itself, or may an old enterprise become a new business if new people become engaged in it? That is one question I should like to have answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two kinds of situations envisaged by the resolution One is the

Excess Profits Tax

case of the person who has commenced business after the 24th day of June, 1944, and the other is that of the person who carries on a substantially different business to which subsection 4 of section 5 of this act is applicable, and uses therein physical assets substantially different from those he used in the business he previously carried on. It is difficult, of course, to say when it is "substantially different business", and I suppose that after these situations are worked with for a while they can be decided. If the changes are small it would not be a substantially different business, but if the changes are. great it is a substantially different business. It is a hard section to apply, I will admit.
Yes, but what I am trying to find out is whether the novelty resides only in the business or whether a new owner may bring about a new business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean? Does he mean a company instead of a partnership?

Yes, or take this example: a man is advanced in years; he finds a purchaser for his business; the purchaser is a young man, who has not quite enough money to pay the full purchase price; he incorporates a company which becomes the owner of the business. He sells some of the securities which , he has received, with the proceeds he pays the price. He manages the company that owns the business. Is that a new business? The owner is entirely new.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is talking about the words of the resolution, but I am thinking all the time about the words of the act. In the case where there has been a new owner, that is a commencement of a business. I have read a few times the provisions of the act:
Provided further that where a person, other than a controlled company described by section fifteen A of this act, in the opinion of the minister,
(i) has commenced business after the twenty-sixth day of June, nineteen hundred and forty-four, . . .
In the case of a new owner that person would be commencing business.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After that date.
Then, if I have correctly understood the minister, that would be a new business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would think that, under the law as it stands, if a person goes into business for the first time be certainly is commencing business.
There is no doubt about that, but is he commencing a new business within the discretion of the minister, who will be the final arbiter in this matter?
That is the problem.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think he is commencing a new business.

Well, "a new business" or "substantially different business".
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, this is what I have in mind. Some years ago there was a case with which the gentlemen administering the income tax are familiar. It was the Pioneer Laundry case; it had to do with depreciation. A company went into bankruptcy; a new company acquired the assets and sought in the ordinary course of business to depreciate, if my memory serves me well, the assets which it had acquired. The court denied that right. Ultimately the privy council held that the company which owned the assets was entitled to depreciation. It held that the discretion of the minister in that case was a judicial discretion and had to be exercised according to judicial principles. I believe that the income tax act was subsequently amended in such a way that depreciation was denied to a company if its shareholders, in the opinion of the minister, had been owners to a substantial degree, possibly to the extent of a majority, of the shares of. the company which had owned the business previously. I have felt that the amendment incorporates a dangerous principle into the law, because it leaves the imposition of a tax subject to the whim of the taxing agent. It seem^ to me that this resolution 5 is an attempt to incorporate into this power to tax the same, as I consider it, pernicious principle that has been incorporated into the sections dealing with depreciation.
I fear that it will get the department into difficulty because it enables the minister to exercise a power which conflicts with the whole scheme of our legislation and jurisprudence. It is going to make a corporation subject to tax or free from tax because of the incident of shareholding in that corporation. It will mean that to-day the corporation is taxable because A and B own shares; tomorrow it w'ill not be taxable because A and B have sold their shares to C and D. That is a hazardous anad unsound principle on which to rest a tax law. For that reason I ask the minister to reconsider this resolution. It makes it possible to overtake somebody who may have escaped taxation last year, but the minister is not only jeopardizing the

Excess Profits Tax
respect which I think everybody has for the department, but incorporating into the legislation a dangerous principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can take one of two
courses. Serious objections have been taken to this resolution. If the committee will let it go through I will promise to consider both of those principles. If they prefer to have it stand I shall let it stand. However, I should like to get at the bill; I should like to decide on some of the sections, and have the bill printed and distributed.

I am quite willing to accept the suggestion of the minister that he will do what he can to meet the objections which he admits are serious. I again say, do iot let the minister undermine the good repute of his own department by going back on legislation which was passed a year or two ago.

There are a couple of things I should like to get clear in my own mind. I realize that this is quite a technical legal argument; I make no pretence of knowing boo much about the law; the only thing I know about it is that any time you find it necessary to have lawyers you pay plenty for them. If you do not have the money you do not get any action.
I am sorry; that is not true.
It is true. That is based on forty years' experience-
I do not care what it is based on; it is not true.
-on the wrong side of the tracks.
Order.
I am sorry; it is not true.
I do not blame those who make a living at it for protesting so loudly.
You come to me and I shall give you some cheap law. It may be worth just what it will cost 'you.
It will be dear at any price.
Now you are getting nasty.
This is a very nice-looking little resolution. There is so much protest from my right that it makes me suspicious that the minister is right.
Now he knows he is wrong.

I should like to ask my hon. friends this question: What constitutes new business in Canada to-day? Perhaps seventy-47696-175J
five per cent of the_ industrial set-up of this country, on the arguments I have listened to, can be classified as new business. The Canada Car and Foundry company have been in war production; they are reconverting their plant to peace-time production; it is a new business.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes. According to the arguments I have listened to, every war plant in this country which is transforming its plant. from the war machine to its ordinary-business of peace-time production can be-classified as starting a new business.
Ask the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I shall confine my remarks to only one point; and may I just tell my hon. friend from the coal mining area of Cape Breton how much I appreciated what he said about my profession. At least he proved himself one of those persons who have not benefited by the advice that has been given; and I am sure the branch down there of the union to which I belong will prosecute him for engaging in the practice of law without being a registered person.
I should like to address myself to one point in connection with resolution 5. My point is this. All legislatures, all parliaments are opposed to retroactive legislation, broadly speaking, and it is only used to correct an obvious and notorious situation. Some English judge whose name I do not recall, although I know he was of the same nationality as the hon. member for Cape Breton South, once made a very wise statement which has never been challenged. He said it was better that ten guilty men should go free than that one innocent man should be convicted. That statement has never been disputed by anyone in the courts of our country or by any of our thinking people.
Obviously resolution 5 means this. The minister at least implied-I was going to say "said"-.that certain smart people' who engaged smart lawyers-apparently I do not belong to that class because I was not so engaged-avoided the intent of the legislation, of 1944. I aim quite sure the gentleman who sits in front of the minister discovered that, and hence we are now met with new legislation. I am in favour of the idea; I am in favour of that broad principle, but I still have enough confidence in the efficacy and soundness of the rule of law to say that even if a few morally dishonest people did escape, it ill becomes this parliament at this time to say to all other persons, "You, too, will be examined. You, too, will be punished."
There is not much difference between criminal legislation and punitive legislation. The municipal councils, the provincial legislatures in our country have power to establish certain penalties for infractions of bytlaws and provincial enactments. The distinction is not very great between a person guilty of a breach of the criminal code and a person guilty of a bregch of a provincial statute, say a liquor act, if you like, since I know something about those, largely on the side of the prosecution. Punitive statutes and criminal statutes have

come very close together. This cannot be interpreted otherwise than as a punitive statute or we would not have it here. There can be no other reason for it except to say, "You smarty-pants beat us in our intention. You lived up to the law but you beat us in our intention. Now we are going back, and we are going to catch you." There can be no other reason for the retroactive feature in this legislation. So that I say to the minister, for whose ability I have great respect-in fact I think he might have advised the hon. member for Cape Breton South at some time or another, for the hon. gentleman certainly got excellent training somewhere-that we should not leave the broad principle. This country, this civilization is founded on law. We live by law, not by an incident of the moment, not by a happy thought we get; and law will always have difficulties in it. It must be of general application. Up there someone will gain a little; down here someone will lose a little, but inasmuch as the law is of general application, let it continue to speak as of the day of its enactment which, in this case, with great respect I submit was the date of the, presentation of the budget. I do not want people to escape, but if they have done so we have a long time to go with those people and we may catch up to them in some-other way. But let law speak as from its date of enactment.
