Excess Profits Tax Act amendment, which states:
That the exemption of the profits of corporations derived from the operation of any base metal or strategic mineral mines be extended to the profits of corporations derived from the operation of gold mines and industrial mineral mines, and that such exemption be extended to the profits of such mines which come into production after January 1, 1946.
This states that exemption under the Excess Profits Tax Act, under certain restrictions, is to be given for a limited period of time. We have already explained to the minister that when the Department of National Revenue apply their ruling this proposal is advantageous only to the high-grade producers. I believe I made that clear in the brief I presented to the Department of Finance. I believe, too, that they have listened to that argument. I have no doubt; in fact I think no one has a doubt that so far as the Department of Finance is concerned in this matter, it has applied the provisions to the gold mining industry, generally speaking. But when it comes to be applied to the Department of National Revenue, the so-called benefits the producers are supposed to get from the legislation is lost.
To low-grade or medium grade gold mines this exemption is absolutely useless. I say this sincerely. Perhaps I should address that statement to the Minister of National Revenue, who possesses good practical knowledge of mining, but I do not wish to repeat myself, and I do not wish to get to my feet again before the session is over, as I realize and understand the mood of the committee at this time of the session.
It looks as though the government is proffering something to the ordinary new producer which is worthless and is not costing the government anything. I say that deliberately, and I wish to make my point clear. Our gold mining industry showed prior to the war, and particularly during the war, that it was willing and ready to pay all the taxes that the government thought fit to impose upon it. It did that in the past, and it is doing so at the present time. No doubt it will continue to do so in the future.
But I repeat that there are certain features in connection with depletion allowance which to some extent are absolutely nullified by the Department of National Revenue. So far as my information goes, the future of mining in our north country is largely dependent upon the willingness of our taxing authorities to provide a fair depletion allowance which will permit an investor, when he makes good, to get his original capital back without us being taxed.
Everyone realizes that mining is highly speculative, and gold mining particularly. I believe that only one man out of ten makes any profit out of the business, and that is a

fair average. I know whereof I speak. I know, too, that many hon. members have in the past invested in some new ventures in gold mining, or even base metals,, and I will leave it to them just how great a return th,ey have received after making, in some instances, a heavy investment.
This provision gives discretionary powers to the Minister of National Revenue, and requires no change in the legislation.
That is all I wish to state at the present time. I am appreciative that hon. members have listened to me. I wish also to make a further statement respecting the Minister of Finance, regardless of what I may have said during the debate on the speech from the throne. Every hon. member on this and on the opposition side of the house knows the fine and gigantic job the Minister of Finance has done in his department during war time. Everyone who has seen him function must realize that the job was a difficult one, but his accomplishments have been admired and appreciated by all those that know of them. It was far from easy. No doubt great credit must be given to him personally for the wonderful things which we have done in our Canadian scheme of financing, and which are the cause of the great confidence that his-actions have inspired.
The workers, the muckers and those in an administrative capacity in my section of the country realize that the Minister of Finance is absolutely open-minded when we bring to his attention something that is .logical. Again I thank the minister and the premiers of the different provinces who attended: the dominion-provincial conference for having found it possible to discuss -this matter. This is one place in which the Department of Finance could give a lead. It can ask what was done in the big mining convention when the ministers of mines of the nine different provinces of the Canadian federation spoke along the same lines as I speak to-night, and also with unanimity.
They realized, and every citizen must realize what will be accomplished by mining. In my own section of Ontario, Quebec and in northern Manitoba and other parts of northern Canada one can see some of the greatest developments, not only in connection with gold mining but in connection with the mining of all kinds of minerals that the world has ever seen.
One has only to look at the map of Canada and know of the regions involved to see that within a few short years many more new mines will be opened and developed fruitfully in those parts of the country. This will be a very great factor in our development. It will be a wonderful factor in the life of every Canadian because, as was stated just

Excess Profits Tax
a few days ago in the committee on external affairs, time after time one person who is employed in mining will give employment to twelve other persons. This has been said by witnesses who knew mining in general. I know the government, and particularly the Minister of Finance are heart and soul behind our means of employment. He has seen for himself, personally, some of our mines. He has seen new sections of the population, such as are found at Timmins, Schumacher, South Porcupine, Kirkland Lake and many other new fine centres in northern Ontario and Quebec. He knows that section, in the same way as it was known by Mr. Crerar, who formerly was Minister of Mines and Resources. I know, too, that in the rehabilitation period gold mining in particular, and mining in general will perform a great national duty, and we hope that all possible attention may be given to the survival and 'extension of this industry. It will prove such a wonderful cure for employment that problems and grivances should be fully'understood, and dealt with in a practical way by the federal government.

I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Cochrane on what he has just said. I can agree with him on everything with the exception of his sanguine thought that the Minister of Finance really appreciates what the mining industry has done, is doing and is capable of doing for the economy of this country. Resolution 6 brings gold mines under the same agreement as the base metal, or what were known during the war as the strategic metal mines, and gives a three-year income tax exemption to new gold mines. I should like to refer for a moment to the original Excess Profits Tax Act and quote a submission which was given to me with regard to section 6, which is as follows:
The exemption as proposed by item 6 of the excess profits tax resolutions will be for the period that the excess profits tax remains in force.	.
The only tax administered by this division which will be payable will be the income tax which at present is 18 per cent of net profits.
Under the procedure adopted in administering the original section 7 (g) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, no set period was allowed for "tuning up" hut you will note that the exemption commences from the time that the property commences production of ore in reasonable commercial quantities. A "tuning up" period of six months was allowed for the purposes of section 89 of the Income War Tax Act in respect of base and precious metal mines but in view of the inclusion of industrial mineral mines under the present proposed legislation, it is not felt that a definite period can be set at this time. -
The "tuning up" provision is purely _ an administrative ruling designed to allow time for the property to come into commercial production.	.
A reasonable enough submission in itself, but I wish to go one step farther. While the announced intention of the act was to provide encouragement or assistance to all mines entering production in the period concerned, the subsequent regulations-these are the words I wish to bring out to the Minister of Finance-issued under the authority of the minister, as provided for in section 4 of the Income War Tax Act, which reads:
The minister may make any regulations deemed necessary for carrying this section into effect.
These have the effect of denying those benefits to any mine, except such as would have been successful in any event. These regulations made it obligatory for all new mines coming under the pro-visions to charge up to production expenses a maximum of fifteen per cent depreciation per annum on their total plant expenses and additionally to charge off annually during the same period a minimum of fifteen per cent of the total predevelopment expenditures made in preparing the mine for production. This is what I brought to the attention of the minister this afternoon when I said I was going to discuss this part of the act.
A low-grade mine may find itself in the position of having to spend as much or even more money in developing its ore body prior to production than it will spend on its whole treatment plant. It is not uncommon to find that when the treatment plant, which may be depreciated at fifteen per cent per annum, costs half a million dollars, a similar sum has been expended on pre-development and must be written off at the same rate. The write-offs that are required to be made in such a case, whether the mine has a profit or not, amount to fifteen per cent of SI million per annum, or $150,000 a year, giving a total of $450,000 in three years. In other words, before any benefits accrue from the release from taxation, such a mine must first make sufficient operating profits to meet these enforced write-offs, a situation that exists only in the larger higher grade mines.
If insufficient profits-this is the case of a loss-to take care of these write-offs are made in the period, then the mine finds itself forced to set up a loss which cannot be applied to reduced future profits. If, therefore, it is really the intention of the government to provide by this means some real assistance and encouragement to new mines to go into production, the present limitation by regulation of depreciation and pre-development write-offs should be entirely removed. If that action is not taken, the effect of the act itself is simply to give to the mines that already have and take from those that need help.

I congratulate the hon. member for Cochrane, who represents a good mining constituency, upon his support of the industry to-night, as I believe that the mining industry in this country is much misunderstood. The general opinion is that anybody connected with mining becomes a millionaire overnight. The mining industry has a definite place in the economic life of this country, and in support of that assertion I should like to read a statement which was made by the former minister of mines, Hon. J. A. Crerar, in April, 1936. He said:
I must emphasize this factor of capital. Few laymen are aware of the vast sums of money required to develop mines. The great deposits of the Flin Flon, in Manitoba, required an expenditure of $30 million before there was any return on this large investment. The mine at Noranda in Quebec required $25 million to enable it 'to produce the refined metals in the large quantity it now does.
I ask the committee to bear this in mind:
The average gold mine takes from $1,000,000 to $5,000,000 to develop and equip to the state of production. Much money must be risked in the early stages of development, for there is no certainty of success. Courageous capital is thus an essential to new mining enterprise.
I would point out to the minister that in a brief which he received from the Mining Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, I think last year, the following statistics were given: that, of Canada's 1942 metal production value, 56 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered prior to 1910, 28 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered between 1910 and 1920, 11 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered between 1920 and 1930, and only 5 per cent was derived from mineral areas 'discovered subsequent to 1930.
I gave some figures this afternoon regarding the industry; and with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I wish to stay fairly close to my 47696-176

The Ontario metal mining industry has been responsible for the establishment of new, prosperous communities, non-existent a few years ago, which, according to the 1941 dominion census, had a combined population of 138,110. Of this total it is estimated that at least 125,000, or 90 per cent, are directly dependent upon metal mining.
I was surprised to find, in reading the budget resolution, that the Minister of Finance gave very little consideration to the metal mining industry of this country. It is estimated, and it appears in the brief of the Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, that for every one person actually engaged in the mining industry in this dominion, twelve other Canadians depend upon the prosperity of that industry for their livelihood. In 1941, the annual report on mineral production issued by the dominion bureau of statistics shows that 113,227 persons were employed in the Canadian mining industry. Taking an average of twelve people employed directly or supported indirectly by the mining industry, we arrive at the figure of 1,358,724 Canadians who owe their livelihood or their living to the success of the mining industry. This figure represents approximately eleven per cent of the population of'the dominion. South Africa is still the leading gold-producing country of the world, but I can see where Canada, with a little encouragement from the Department of Finance-and after all it is only his department that can encourage the industry-can be put in the position of leading the world in gold production. If we reach that position we shall be creating new wealth, and new wealth in connection with mining means jobs for very many people in this country.
Gold mines in this country produce new wealth and create markets for foodstuffs, labour, lumber, electricity, transportation and services of all kinds, and I would remind the minister that gold mines pay very heavy taxes to the dominion treasury. I would also remind the minister and his officials, however, that gold mines cannot reproduce themselves. Once a level in a mine is mined out it is gone for good. Neither the minister nor anyone else can put gold back in the ground. The life of the average Canadian gold mine is only about eight years. We are very fortunate in that, for many miles across our country we have the pre-Cambrian shield which statistics show has been prospected only to about ten per cent.
I would again ask the minister to show consideration for this industry, which means so much not only to Ontario but to every prov-

Canada has been fortunate over the past fifteen years, in that the price of gold has shown a substantial increase; and I wish to show what that increase has meant to this country. In terms of new jobs, new payrolls, new wealth and the actual amount of gold mined, this is what happens with a rise in gold prices. Between 1930 and 1939 the price received by Canadian mines for their gold rose as a result of currency exchange fluctuations from 820.67 per ounce, to 836.14 per ounce. Compiled from the records of seven Ontario mines which were in steady production during the period from 1930 to 1939 the price of gold went up seventy-four per cent. The tons of ore milled went up fifty-two per cent; the ounces of gold recovered went up'thirteen per cent; the proportion of recovery in ounces of gold per ton milled went down twenty-six per cent, and the total number of our employed increased by 161 per cent. That meant, Mr. Chairman, that because of the increase in the price of gold the mining industry were able to treat many more tons of lower grade ore than they were able to treat in the years gone by. This lower grade ore gave much employment directly and indirectly in this country. I wish to tell the committee what this increase in the price of gold meant. With the higher price of gold the mining industry produced thirteen per cent more ounces of gold from fifty-two per cent more tons of ore, and the seven mines that are referred to in the statement mined and milled 1,489,052 more tons of ore than they did in 1930. Because of the increase in the price of gold the mining industry was able to treat many more tons of ore, and the lumbering, transportation, electricity and every other kind of industries throughout Canada benefited.
Those of us who are connected with the mining industry believe that we have a very sound case, and we ask the minister to go back to the point where the industry was many years ago when it was allowed a fifty peT cent depletion allowance, and the shareholders received a similar allowance when the dividends came into their hands. If we are to develop our gold mining industry the minister must realize that the people who put their money into the industry take great risks. If it is a gold mining company it is using the shareholder's money to develop further prospecting. I would again ask the minister to consider this whole question of mining taxation. If I can be of any assistance to the officials of the department I shall be only too 47696-1764
glad to do anything I can. I believe that the-future of this country in good times and in bad depends on the success of that industry which has done so much to carry us through , depression years and war years.
